Workers knock and announce themselves, protect privacy during personal care, ask before touching or moving belongings, and offer choices. They do not impose their own preferences. The Home Services Supervisor checks these practices at each supervisory visit.

A client may decline any task or visit. The worker respects the refusal, tells the Home Services Supervisor the same day, and documents it. The supervisor explains any health or safety consequences to the client and updates the plan if the client wishes.
A client may ask for a different worker. The Home Services Supervisor responds within [NUMBER] business days and tries to assign a different worker without penalty.
Clients may not be restrained, secluded or made to stay in their home, and may not be denied visitors or contact with others, by agency workers.

For CCP and HSP clients, the Home Services Supervisor reviews the client's care plan with the Care Coordination Unit or DHS-DRS counselor, and makes sure no agency practice limits the client's choice, privacy or access to the community. Any restriction in the plan must be approved by the program.

A worker who sees a rights violation, or who is asked by a client to report one, reports it to the Home Services Supervisor immediately. Abuse, neglect or exploitation is reported under SAF-01. Complaints are handled under CR-02.
Retaliation against a client or a worker for raising a rights concern is prohibited and is grounds for discipline up to termination.
The Agency Manager reviews rights-related complaints and supervisory findings quarterly and reports trends to the QI committee (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains this policy, the rights notice and the rights training content, and reviews rights trends quarterly.
Explains and obtains acknowledgement of the rights notice at intake.
Involves the client and representative in the service plan, observes worker practice, and responds to refusals and requests for a change of worker.
Respect client rights during every visit and report concerns to the supervisor.
Takes part in planning, gives accurate information and tells the agency of concerns.

documentation: Signed rights and responsibilities acknowledgement in the client record.
Service plan showing client and representative participation.
Client agreement with termination terms and complaint contact information.
Records of refusals, requests for a different worker and the agency's response.
Annual rights training records.
Supervisory visit notes on rights observations.

policies.title: Grievances and Complaints
policies.applies_to: All clients, client representatives and client advocates who raise a concern, and all agency staff who receive or resolve one.
policies.purpose: To give clients, representatives and advocates a clear, fair and prompt way to raise concerns about [AGENCY NAME], and to ensure each concern is recorded, resolved and used to improve services.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has a written complaint-resolution policy that covers the agency, its clients and client advocates. Each client receives, in the written agreement, contact information for concerns, complaints and questions. Every complaint is logged, investigated, answered and used in the QI evaluation. No one is retaliated against for making a complaint. Any client may also contact IDPH, the Care Coordination Unit or DHS-DRS at any time, and the agency will not discourage them from doing so.

definitions.definition: Any expression of dissatisfaction or concern about the agency, its services or its staff, whether spoken or written, from a client, representative, advocate or family member.
A person who speaks for or supports a client, such as a family member, ombudsman, case manager or friend.
The agency's record of each complaint with dates, findings and responses.

procedures: At intake, the Intake Coordinator gives the client and representative the complaint contact: [COMPLAINT CONTACT NAME], [PHONE], [ADDRESS]. This information is in the written client agreement. The Intake Coordinator explains how to make a complaint orally or in writing, and that anonymous complaints are accepted.

The agreement and rights notice also tell the client that they may contact IDPH at 217-782-7412 (TTY 800-547-0466) or DPH.COOS@illinois.gov. For CCP clients, the Senior HelpLine is 1-800-252-8966. For HSP clients, the DHS-DRS counselor may be contacted.

Any employee who receives a complaint writes down what was said, the date, who made it and who it concerns, and gives it to the Home Services Supervisor by the end of the next business day. The employee does not try to resolve it alone or discourage the complainant.
The Home Services Supervisor logs the complaint in the complaint log within 1 business day and gives it a tracking number.
The supervisor contacts the complainant within 2 business days to acknowledge the complaint, confirm the facts and explain the process and expected timeframe.

If a complaint involves a safety risk, abuse, neglect, exploitation or a crime, the supervisor stops and follows SAF-01, SAF-02, SAF-07 or SAF-08 as appropriate. The complaint process continues in parallel.
If the complaint concerns the Home Services Supervisor, the Agency Manager handles it. If it concerns the Agency Manager, the Governing Body handles it.

The investigator gathers facts by interviewing the complainant, the worker and others, and reviewing records such as the visit notes, schedule and service plan. The investigator documents findings and conclusions.

The agency gives the complainant a written response within [NUMBER] business days that states the findings, any action taken and the right to take the concern to IDPH or the funding program. If more time is needed, the complainant is told why and given a new date.
If the complainant remains dissatisfied, the Agency Manager reviews the complaint and the investigator's findings and gives a final written response.

Corrective actions, such as retraining, a schedule change, a change in worker, a plan update or discipline, are assigned, dated and documented. The supervisor follows up with the client within 30 days to see whether the problem is resolved.

The agency does not retaliate against a client or worker who complains, and does not reduce or end services because a complaint was made. Any suspected retaliation is reported to the Agency Manager immediately.

For clients served through the IDoA Community Care Program or the DHS-DRS Home Services Program, the Home Services Supervisor notifies the Care Coordination Unit or DHS-DRS counselor of any complaint involving their client's care, as the program requires (see SVC-10).
If IDPH contacts the agency about a complaint, the IDPH contact responds the same day and the matter is handled under GOV-08.
The complaint log records the date received, complainant, subject, findings, action taken, response date and outcome. The Agency Manager reviews the log monthly.
Complaint trends are reported to the QI committee each quarter and used in the QI evaluation (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Owns the complaint-resolution policy, handles complaints about the supervisor and reviews the log monthly.
Logs, investigates and resolves complaints and follows up with the client.
Gives complaint contact information to each client and explains how to complain.
Accept, record and forward every complaint and never retaliate.
Analyzes complaint data each quarter.

documentation: Complaint log with dates, findings and responses.
Written complaint record and investigation notes.
Written response to the complainant.
Corrective action and follow-up record.
Client agreement showing complaint contact information.
Quarterly QI report with complaint trends.

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All employees, contracted workers, volunteers and governing body members who have access to client or personnel information in any form.
policies.purpose: To protect the confidentiality of client and personnel information and to set clear rules for the use, removal and release of records.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps client personal, financial and health information confidential. A written confidentiality policy governs the use, removal and release of client records. The office protects the confidentiality of both paper and electronic records. Workers are trained on confidentiality. Personnel records are also kept confidential. Where HIPAA applies, for example because the agency bills Medicaid-funded services electronically or otherwise qualifies as a covered entity, the agency also follows the HIPAA Privacy Rule.

definitions.definition: Any information that identifies a client or relates to the client's health, finances, home, family or services, in any form.
Sharing, examining or analyzing client information inside the agency for the agency's work.
Giving client information to anyone outside the agency.
Individually identifiable health information that is covered by HIPAA when the agency is a covered entity.
Using or releasing only the information needed for the task or purpose.

procedures: The Agency Manager, with counsel, determines whether [AGENCY NAME] is a HIPAA covered entity, and documents the decision. If it is one, the agency adopts HIPAA privacy and security procedures, names a privacy official ([PRIVACY OFFICIAL NAME]), and issues a notice of privacy practices. If it is not, the agency still follows this policy for all client information.
All employees and contracted workers sign a confidentiality statement at hire and before accessing any client or personnel information. Signed statements are kept in the personnel file.

Orientation and annual training cover confidentiality of client personal, financial and health information. Training is documented with the date, topic, minutes, instructor and worker signature (see PER-03).

Staff access client information only when their job requires it and use only the minimum necessary. Staff may not look up records of clients they do not serve, or of family, friends or neighbors, for personal reasons.
The office keeps paper client records in locked cabinets in a room that is locked outside business hours. Only authorized staff hold keys.
Electronic records require individual log-ins, strong passwords and automatic screen locks. Systems are backed up, and access is removed the same day an employee leaves.

Staff do not discuss clients in public places, on social media or with anyone who does not need to know. Texts and personal email are not used for client information unless the agency has approved a secure method.

Client records and paper schedules are not removed from the office except for a documented purpose, such as a supervisory visit, a copy of the service plan left in the client's home, or an approved electronic device. Workers keep these secure at all times, never leave them in a vehicle, and return them the same day.

Records are released only with the client's or representative's signed authorization, except where the law allows or requires release without it. Examples are reporting abuse or neglect, responding to IDPH, the funding program or law enforcement, and a court order. The Agency Manager approves each release.
The authorization states who may receive the information, what is released, the purpose, and an expiration date. The client may revoke it in writing.
Each release is logged with the date, recipient, content, purpose and the staff member who released it. A copy of what was released goes in the client record.
Faxed records go on non-thermal paper. The sender confirms the recipient's fax number before sending and uses a cover sheet with a confidentiality notice.

Personnel records are kept in a locked file or secured electronic system. Access is limited to the Agency Manager, Human Resources and those who need it. Employees may review their own file on request with notice.
Client records are kept at least 2 years after the last date of service and are destroyed afterward by shredding or secure electronic deletion (see REC-01 and REC-03).

A worker who finds or causes a breach, such as a lost record, a misdirected email, or unauthorized access, reports it to the Agency Manager immediately, and in all cases within 24 hours. The Agency Manager investigates, limits the harm, notifies affected clients and any required authorities within the time the law requires, and records the event as an incident (see SAF-02).
Violation of this policy leads to discipline up to termination. Staff who report violations in good faith are protected from retaliation.
The Agency Manager reviews this policy annually and after any breach (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Determines HIPAA status, approves record releases, investigates breaches and reviews the policy annually.
If HIPAA applies, handles privacy complaints, the notice of privacy practices and breach assessment.
Collects confidentiality statements and protects personnel records.
Protect client information, use the minimum necessary, and report breaches the same day.

documentation: Signed confidentiality statements.
HIPAA covered-entity determination and any privacy notice and procedures.
Signed client authorizations and release log.
Confidentiality training records.
Breach and incident reports.
Record destruction log.

policies.title: Client Property, Gifts and Financial Exploitation Prevention
policies.applies_to: All employees, contracted workers and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME] who enter a client's home or handle a client's money, property or financial information.
policies.purpose: To protect clients' property and money, set clear rules on gifts, loans and use of client funds, and make sure any suspected financial exploitation is reported and investigated.
policies.policy: Workers must respect and protect client property. Financial exploitation is a reportable event and is handled through the same channels as abuse and neglect. Workers may not accept gifts of money or valuables, borrow from or lend to clients, use client funds or cards for personal purposes, or take part in a client's will or financial affairs. Shopping and household-records tasks require receipts and a reconciliation record. Any worker accused of exploitation is removed from direct client contact immediately while the agency investigates.

definitions.definition: The illegal, unauthorized or improper use of a client's money, property, assets or credit for the benefit of someone other than the client, including through deception, coercion or undue influence.
Cash, checks, debit, credit or EBT cards, account information, and any other money or financial instruments belonging to the client.
Money, property or anything of value given to a worker by a client or client's family, other than the agreed payment for services.
A written account of money given to and spent by a worker for a client, with receipts and the change returned.

procedures: At hire and annually, every worker receives and signs this policy. Orientation and annual training include the behaviors that constitute abuse, neglect and financial exploitation and how to report them (see PER-03 and SAF-01).

Workers do not accept cash, checks, gift cards, jewelry or other valuables from clients or family members. A nominal, non-monetary item of no more than $10 in value, such as a homemade snack, may be accepted. The worker tells the Home Services Supervisor, who notes it in the record.
Workers do not borrow money or property from clients, lend money to clients, sell items to clients, ask for tips, or take part in raffles or fundraisers with clients.

Workers do not accept appointment as a client's power of attorney, executor, guardian or beneficiary, do not witness a will or sign legal or financial documents for the client, and do not help change legal or financial documents.
Workers do not use client funds, cards, bank accounts, PINs or passwords for any personal purpose, and do not keep copies of this information.
The agency does not permit workers to handle client money unless the service plan authorizes shopping or errands. The service plan states the task, who provides the money and the limit per trip.

When shopping, the worker counts the cash with the client before leaving and records the amount on the agency's shopping log. The worker gets an itemized receipt, returns the receipt and change to the client, and has the client sign the log. If the client cannot sign, the worker documents that and another adult is asked to verify when possible.
Workers keep client funds separate from their own and never put them in a personal account or wallet.

For household records tasks, such as sorting mail or organizing bills, workers keep the client's papers in the client's home, do not sign for the client, do not pay bills with their own accounts and do not keep copies.

Workers report any missing money or property to the Home Services Supervisor the same day. The supervisor documents what was missing, when it was last seen and who had access, and helps the client look for it. If it is not found, the supervisor reports it under SAF-02 and considers whether to notify police.

Workers who notice signs of exploitation, such as unexplained withdrawals, new names on accounts, pressure from others to sign documents, missing belongings, unpaid bills despite adequate income, or a client who cannot explain their finances, report it to the Home Services Supervisor immediately.

On reasonable suspicion of financial exploitation of a client aged 60 or older, a client with a disability, or any eligible adult, the agency notifies the elder abuse provider agency designated by IDoA or the Area Agency on Aging. For a client under 18, the agency calls the DCFS Child Abuse Hotline. The report is documented and kept on the premises for 12 months (see SAF-01).

Employees and volunteers also report their concern directly to management and to the elder abuse provider agency or IDoA. Mandated-reporter duties apply to individuals and are not satisfied by telling a supervisor alone.

If the alleged perpetrator is an employee, the Agency Manager removes the employee from all direct client contact immediately and begins an investigation. A written investigation report is completed within 14 days of the initial report, and sent to IDPH within 24 hours after the investigation is completed. A copy is kept for 12 months (see SAF-08).
If a crime may have been committed by another person in the home, the supervisor calls 911 or local police immediately (see SAF-07).

The Agency Manager reviews gift and shopping logs and exploitation concerns quarterly and reports to the QI committee (see GOV-04). Violation of this policy leads to discipline up to termination and may be referred to law enforcement.

responsibilities.duty: Enforces this policy, removes accused employees from client contact, directs the investigation and files required reports.
Writes shopping and money authorization into the service plan, reviews logs and receipts, and receives reports of missing property and concerns.
Follow gift, loan and money rules, keep receipts and logs, and report suspected exploitation.
Obtains signed acknowledgements and tracks training.

documentation: Signed policy acknowledgement by each worker.
Service plan entry authorizing any shopping or errands with money limits.
Shopping log and reconciliation record with receipts.
Gift disclosures to the supervisor.
Missing property reports.
Abuse, neglect and exploitation report, kept 12 months, and the written investigation report.
Training records on abuse, neglect and exploitation.

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Language Access
policies.applies_to: All employees, contracted staff, supervisors, the Agency Manager and the governing body
federal: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act (42 USC 2000d)
policies.purpose: To make sure no one is refused service or treated differently because of a protected characteristic, and that clients and applicants with limited English proficiency, hearing loss, other disabilities or dementia can understand and take part in decisions about their care.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not refuse service to any person because of actual or perceived race, color, religion, national origin, ancestry, age, sex, marital status, order of protection status, disability, military status, sexual orientation, pregnancy or unfavorable military discharge, as listed in 775 ILCS 5/1-103(Q) and referenced in the acceptance and discharge rule at 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(d). The agency's personnel policies require compliance with the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.30(c)(1)(F)). The agency provides communication assistance at no cost to clients and applicants, and trains workers to communicate with people who are hard of hearing or have dementia (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.71(e)). The same standards apply to hiring, assignment, discipline and discharge of employees.

definitions.definition: A characteristic listed in 775 ILCS 5/1-103(Q): actual or perceived race, color, religion, national origin, ancestry, age, sex, marital status, order of protection status, disability, military status, sexual orientation, pregnancy or unfavorable military discharge.
A person whose primary language is not English and who has a limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English.
Help that gives people with hearing, vision or speech disabilities effective communication, such as a sign language interpreter, large-print or Braille materials, or written notes.

A person who is fluent in both languages, understands confidentiality, and interprets accurately and impartially. A client's family member or friend is not used unless the client asks for that person, and the request is documented.

procedures: The Agency Manager reviews this policy with every new employee during orientation, and the employee signs an acknowledgment that is filed in the personnel record.

Intake staff decide whether to accept a client based only on the client's need for non-medical help, staff availability in the service area and the agency's ability to meet the documented needs. Protected-class characteristics are never a factor.

If an applicant is declined for any reason, the intake coordinator records the specific non-discriminatory reason (for example, needs are skilled or no trained worker is available) on the intake form and the Agency Manager reviews and signs the decision within 2 business days.
At first contact, intake staff ask each applicant and representative what language they prefer and whether they need any communication aid. The answer is recorded in the client record.

For clients with LEP, the agency arranges a qualified interpreter or translated materials through [INTERPRETER OR LANGUAGE LINE VENDOR] at no cost to the client. The service agreement, service plan, client rights notice and grievance procedure are explained in the client's language.
Staff do not use a minor child as an interpreter. A family member or friend interprets only at the client's request, and the request is documented.

For clients who are hard of hearing, have limited vision or have another disability affecting communication, the supervisor identifies the needed aid (for example, large print, written summaries, captioned or relay telephone, or an in-person interpreter) during the assessment and lists it on the service plan.
Workers are trained during orientation on communicating with people who are hard of hearing or have dementia, and on respectful communication across cultures. Training is documented under PER-03.

The agency makes reasonable modifications to its policies where needed so people with disabilities can receive services, unless the change would require the agency to provide medical services or services outside Part 245. Requests and decisions are recorded in the client record.
Workers may not make remarks, jokes or comments about a client's or co-worker's protected characteristics, and may not treat clients differently because of them.

A worker or client who believes discrimination has occurred reports it to the Agency Manager, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], at [PHONE]. The report is handled under CR-02 (Grievances and Complaints), and the agency does not retaliate against anyone who reports.
The Agency Manager investigates each discrimination allegation, documents findings and corrective action within 14 days of receipt, and informs the complainant of the outcome.
Employment discrimination complaints against managers are referred to the governing body for review.
The Agency Manager reviews interpreter use, declined referrals and discrimination complaints each quarter and reports the results to the Quality Improvement committee (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy, reviews discrimination complaints involving management, and ensures resources are available for interpreter and communication services.
Ensures nondiscrimination in intake, hiring and discipline, reviews declined referrals, investigates complaints and arranges language and communication services.
Asks about language and communication needs, records reasons for any declined referral, and arranges interpreters.
Identifies communication needs during assessment, builds them into the service plan, and monitors workers' respectful practice during supervisory visits.
Treat all clients with respect, use communication aids as planned and report discrimination concerns.

documentation: Employee acknowledgment of this policy (personnel record)
Intake form showing language preference, communication needs and reason for any declined referral
Interpreter or translation service log and any client request to use a family interpreter
Service plan section listing communication aids
Discrimination complaint file and investigation outcome
Orientation training records on communication with people who are hard of hearing or have dementia
Quarterly review summary for the Quality Improvement committee

policies.title: Service Agreement, Rates and Billing Disclosure
policies.applies_to: Agency Manager, intake and scheduling staff, billing staff and supervisors
policies.purpose: To make sure every client or representative receives, before services begin, a written list of services with the scope of each, a signed agreement containing all required terms, and a clear statement of charges, who pays and when.
policies.policy: Before contracting with a client, [AGENCY NAME] gives the client the list of services it offers and the scope of work for each. The agency gives the list again with the signed contract and whenever the list changes (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(a)). No services begin until a written client agreement has been signed. The agreement includes the six items required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(c): assurance of compliance with the Act, including the Health Care Worker Background Check Act; who pays employment taxes, Social Security taxes and workers' compensation; who supervises workers and who hires, fires and disciplines them; charges, payment schedule and payee; contract term and conditions for termination; and contact information for concerns, complaints and questions. For clients paid through the IDoA Community Care Program or the DHS-DRS Home Services Program, the program rate governs, and the agency does not bill the client for any difference unless the program permits it.

definitions.definition: The agency's written list of the non-medical services it offers (for example, ADL support, personal care, medication reminding, housekeeping, laundry, cooking, shopping, transport to appointments, household records and companionship) with the scope of work for each.
The signed written contract between the agency and the client or representative that states the terms required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(c).
The Illinois Department on Aging program for older persons. In-home service (S5130) is paid at $30.80 per hour statewide, or $32.57 per hour with insurance, under the rates effective 1/1/2026.

The DHS-DRS program for people with severe disabilities under age 60. Current maximum unit prices include homemaker (4100) at $30.80 per hour, personal assistant (4150) at $20.00 per hour and non-agency CNA (4198) at $23.00 per hour, as updated 7/1/2026.
Services paid for by the client, family or private insurance rather than through CCP or HSP.

procedures: The Agency Manager approves and maintains the agency's current list of services and the scope of work for each. The list is reviewed whenever services are added or removed, and at least annually under GOV-03.
At first inquiry, and before any contract is discussed, intake staff give the client or representative the current list of services. The date and method of delivery are recorded on the intake form.
Intake staff explain which services the agency does not provide, including skilled nursing or medical care, and refer the client elsewhere when needed (see SVC-01).
Before the first visit, the Agency Manager or designee reviews the client agreement with the client or representative in a language and format they understand (see CR-05) and answers questions.
The agreement states that [AGENCY NAME] complies with the Health Care Worker Background Check Act and the Home Health, Home Services, and Home Nursing Agency Licensing Act.

The agreement states that [AGENCY NAME] is the employer of its home services workers and pays employment taxes, Social Security taxes and workers' compensation insurance. If any worker is provided by a third party under contract, the agreement says so and states who pays those costs.

The agreement states that [AGENCY NAME], through its supervisors and Agency Manager, supervises workers and hires, disciplines and terminates them. Clients may report concerns but do not direct employment actions.

For private-pay clients, the agreement lists the hourly rate of [HOURLY RATE], any minimum visit length, any different rates for holidays or other special conditions, how and when invoices are issued, the payment due date and the payee, [AGENCY NAME].

For CCP clients, the agreement states that [AGENCY NAME] is paid by the program at the program rate (currently $30.80 per hour statewide, or $32.57 per hour with insurance, effective 1/1/2026) and that the client is not billed for the rate. Any client cost-sharing or participation amount set by the program is stated exactly as assigned by the program.
For HSP clients, the agreement states the unit price and service code under which the agency is paid. Unit prices are set by DHS-DRS and are not changed by the agency.

The agency does not charge CCP or HSP clients any amount over the program rate unless the program expressly permits it. Before any such charge, the Agency Manager obtains written confirmation of that permission from the program and documents it in the client record.
The agreement states the contract term, how long notice is required to end it, and the conditions under which the agency or client may terminate. These must be consistent with SVC-09.

The agreement lists contact information for concerns, complaints and questions: the Agency Manager, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], [PHONE], and the Illinois Department of Public Health Home Services Program, 217-782-7412 (TTY 800-547-0466). It also describes the process in CR-02.

The client or representative signs and dates the agreement and receives a copy. The agency retains the signed original in the client record before the first visit. Any missing signature must be resolved before services start.

When rates, services or any required term changes, the Agency Manager gives written notice to the client or representative before the change takes effect and obtains a signed updated agreement or acknowledgment. If the list of services changes, a new copy is provided.

Billing staff issue invoices or program claims only for services documented as delivered, and reconcile each invoice against visit records and EVV data (see SVC-07 and GOV-05). Billing errors are corrected and any overpayment is returned or credited promptly.

The Agency Manager audits a sample of client records each quarter to confirm that a signed agreement, a service list acknowledgment and correct rate information are on file, and reports results under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Approves the list of services, the agreement template and rates, signs off that agreements are complete, and handles questions on charges.
Gives the services list before contracting, reviews the agreement with the client and obtains signatures.
Bill only for documented services at the correct rate, never bill program clients for rate differences unless permitted, and correct errors.
Confirms that service delivered matches the agreement and plan, and refers client questions about charges to the Agency Manager.
Approves private-pay rates and the agreement template and reviews audit results.

documentation: Current list of services and scope of work for each, with revision dates
Record of date and method the services list was given before contracting, with the signed contract, and after each change
Signed client agreement and copy provided to the client
Rate sheet and effective dates for private-pay clients
CCP or HSP authorization and rate documentation
Written program permission for any permitted client charge above the program rate
Notices of rate or service changes and signed acknowledgments
Invoices, claims and reconciliation records
Quarterly record audit results

policies.title: Scope of Services - What Home Services Workers May and May Not Do
policies.applies_to: All home services workers, supervisors, intake staff and the Agency Manager
policies.purpose: To define clearly the non-medical tasks home services workers may perform, the tasks that require additional conditions, and the tasks workers must never perform, so that clients are safe and the agency stays within its license.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides non-medical home services only. Home services means help with activities of daily living (ADLs), housekeeping, personal laundry and companionship in the client's residence, and excludes anything that requires a Nurse Practice Act licensee (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.40(c)(1)). The agency may not provide medical services, meaning services a home health or home nursing agency would provide (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(d)). Workers perform only the tasks permitted by Part 245 and listed in the client's service plan. Workers may observe and report changes in client functioning, do chores and meal preparation, help with shopping and appointments, provide companionship, document services, and assist with ADLs and personal care (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.40(c)(3)). Tasks that carry extra conditions are performed only when the conditions in SVC-11 are met. Workers do not perform skilled skin care, wound care, dressing changes, tube or syringe feeding, nail trimming, passive range of motion, catheter insertion or removal, or medication setup. Workers may remind a client about medications only as described in SVC-05.

definitions.definition: Help with ADLs, housekeeping, personal laundry and companionship in the client's residence. It does not include anything that requires a Nurse Practice Act licensee.
Basic personal care tasks such as bathing, dressing, grooming, eating, toileting, transferring and walking.
A task that requires the judgment or training of a licensed nurse or other licensed professional, such as wound care, dressing changes, injections, catheter care or tube feeding.
Selecting, sorting, pouring, filling or otherwise preparing medications for a client. Workers may never perform or provide it.

A permitted task, such as bathing, positioning, feeding or nail care, that may be done only when conditions are met: client or representative feedback, worker training in the method, an agency competency evaluation and, for some tasks, a health care professional's order.

procedures: The Agency Manager keeps a current written list of the services the agency offers and the scope of work for each (see CR-06). The list may not include any task that requires a Nurse Practice Act licensee.
During intake and assessment, the Home Services Supervisor compares the client's requested tasks to the agency's scope of services and to the tasks permitted in 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.40(c).
The supervisor writes into the service plan only tasks that are within scope. Tasks outside the scope in 245.40(c)(4) may not be listed on the plan (see SVC-03).

For each conditioned task, such as bathing, positioning, feeding, nail care or toileting assistance, the supervisor confirms and documents the client or representative feedback, the worker's training in the method and a completed agency competency evaluation before the worker first performs it, as described in SVC-11. Where a health care professional's order is required, the order is obtained and filed in the client record before the task is performed.
Workers perform only the tasks on the current service plan. A worker may not accept additional or different tasks from the client, family or others without supervisor approval.

Workers do not perform skilled skin care, wound care, dressing changes, tube or syringe feeding, nail trimming, passive range of motion, or catheter insertion or removal, even if a client, family member or physician asks.

Workers do not perform or provide medication setup. A worker may remind a client to take medications only when they have already been pre-selected by the client, a family member, a nurse or a pharmacist and are in containers other than prescription bottles, such as medication minders, as described in SVC-05.

If a client asks a worker to do something outside the plan or scope, the worker politely declines, explains that the agency cannot provide that service, and calls the supervisor at [PHONE] the same day.

The supervisor documents the request, contacts the client or representative within 1 business day, and, if appropriate, helps the client find a licensed home health or home nursing agency or other resource.

Workers observe and report changes in client functioning, such as new confusion, weakness, falls, skin changes, poor appetite or changes in mood, to the supervisor the same day, and immediately for emergencies (see SVC-08).

If a client's condition changes so that needs become skilled, the supervisor arranges a reassessment within 2 business days and informs the client or representative in writing. The agency refers the client to a home health or home nursing agency while continuing to serve non-medical needs only if safe and within scope.
If the agency can no longer safely meet the client's needs within its scope, the Agency Manager follows SVC-09 on discharge, including written notice and a documented reason.
At each visit the worker documents services provided in the client record, and the supervisor reviews documentation to identify tasks done outside the plan.

If a worker is found to have performed an out-of-scope task, the supervisor reports it to the Agency Manager within 1 business day. The Agency Manager ensures the client's safety, determines whether a reportable incident occurred (SAF-02), and takes corrective action up to retraining or discipline.

The Agency Manager reviews scope-of-service questions and out-of-scope events each quarter and reports to the Quality Improvement committee (GOV-04). Any change to the list of services is shared with clients in writing.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the list of services and scope, decides scope questions, reviews out-of-scope events and ensures referral when needs become skilled.
Matches requested tasks to scope, builds a compliant service plan, confirms conditions for conditioned tasks and handles out-of-scope requests.
Perform only plan tasks within scope, decline out-of-scope requests, report changes and document each visit.
Explains the agency's services and limits to applicants and refers those whose needs the agency cannot meet.

documentation: Current list of services and scope of work
Intake and assessment records showing scope review
Service plan listing only permitted tasks
Task conditions records for conditioned tasks: client or representative feedback, training and competency evaluation, and any health care professional order
Worker visit documentation of each service at each visit
Out-of-scope request and event reports with follow-up
Referral notes for clients needing skilled services
Quarterly scope review summary

policies.title: Client Intake, Acceptance and Assessment
policies.applies_to: Intake staff, Home Services Supervisors and the Agency Manager
policies.purpose: To make sure clients are accepted for service based on a documented need for non-medical help, that an assessment of functional limitations and relevant circumstances is completed before service begins, and that no one is refused for a protected reason.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] follows written acceptance and discharge policies as required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(d). A client is accepted based on the client's desire or need for household, personal support or companionship help. The agency does not accept clients who need medical services that a home health or home nursing agency would provide. Acceptance is based on documented functional limitations and relevant circumstances, which the agency records in consultation with the client and the family or representative, including basic information on medications, treatments, activity, diet and mental status. A client who needs complete repositioning and cannot signal may be accepted only if the assigned worker is trained and has had a competency evaluation, and the representative can assist or give feedback. The agency does not refuse anyone for a reason prohibited under 775 ILCS 5/1-103(Q) (see CR-05).

definitions.definition: The process of taking a referral or inquiry, gathering identifying and contact information and deciding whether the agency can meet the person's non-medical needs.

The documented review, done in consultation with the client and family or representative, of functional limitations, circumstances, medications, treatments, activity, diet and mental status that supports acceptance and the service plan.
A person legally authorized to act for the client, such as an agent under a power of attorney or a guardian, or a family member or friend the client has named to take part in planning.
A client who needs complete help with repositioning and cannot reposition or signal for help.

procedures: Intake staff record each referral or inquiry on the intake form, including the client's name, address, phone number, the referral source, the requested services and the date and time of contact.
Intake staff gather identifying information, representative contact information and an emergency contact, and record the payer (private pay, CCP via a Care Coordination Unit, or HSP via DHS-DRS).

Intake staff screen the request against the agency's list of services (SVC-01). If the client needs skilled or medical care the agency cannot provide, the coordinator tells the client or representative and offers referral to a home health or home nursing agency or other resource.
Intake staff confirm the agency has a trained worker and supervisory capacity in the client's location before proposing a start date.

The Home Services Supervisor schedules the in-home assessment with the client and, if the client wishes, family or representative, within [NUMBER] business days of the referral, and sooner when the client's situation is urgent.

At the assessment, the supervisor documents functional limitations and how they relate to the services requested, including mobility, transfers, bathing, dressing, eating, toileting, communication, vision and hearing.

The supervisor also records basic information from the client and family or representative about medications, treatments being received, activity, diet and mental status, including memory or behavior concerns that could point to dementia services under SVC-12.
The supervisor looks at the home environment for hazards to the client and worker (see SAF-05) and notes equipment the client has or needs.

If the client needs complete repositioning and cannot signal, the supervisor confirms before acceptance that the assigned worker has been trained and has passed an agency competency evaluation, and that the representative can assist or give feedback. These facts are documented. If any condition is missing, the client is not accepted until it is met or is referred elsewhere.

The supervisor reviews findings with the Agency Manager, who decides within 2 business days whether to accept the client. The reason for acceptance or non-acceptance is written on the intake form and signed.

No applicant is declined because of race, color, religion, national origin, ancestry, age, sex, marital status, order of protection status, disability, military status, sexual orientation, pregnancy or unfavorable military discharge. The Agency Manager reviews each declined referral for compliance.
When accepting a client, the intake coordinator gives the client the list of services and the client agreement and obtains signatures before service begins (see CR-06).

The supervisor develops the service plan with the client or representative and, if the client wishes, family, and completes it before or at the first visit (see SVC-03). The initial plan and the assessment are filed in the client record.

For CCP and HSP clients, intake staff compare the agency's assessment to the service authorization from the Care Coordination Unit or DHS-DRS worker and notify the referring entity of any difference (see SVC-10).

If the assessment shows a need the agency cannot meet, or a safety issue arises, the supervisor informs the Agency Manager, who decides on next steps, including referral or conditional acceptance with documented safeguards.
The Agency Manager reviews intake and acceptance records quarterly for completeness and for protected-class compliance and reports to the Quality Improvement committee (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Makes and signs acceptance decisions, reviews declined referrals and ensures the agency can meet accepted clients' needs.
Takes referrals, screens against scope, collects identifying and contact information and ensures the agreement is signed before service.
Completes the in-home assessment, documents functional limitations and circumstances, confirms worker training for repositioning clients and develops the plan.
Share observations that help update the assessment and report changes.

documentation: Intake form with referral source, payer, requested services and decision with reason
Identifying information, representative contact and emergency contact
Assessment record of functional limitations, circumstances and basic information on medications, treatments, activity, diet and mental status
Documentation of worker training, competency evaluation and representative availability for any repositioning client
Signed client agreement and services list acknowledgment
Referral records for clients not accepted
Quarterly intake and acceptance review

policies.title: Service Plan and Plan Updates
policies.applies_to: Home Services Supervisors, Agency Manager and home services workers
policies.purpose: To make sure every client has a written service plan developed with the client and others, covering all required content, kept in the client record, and reviewed at least annually and whenever needs change.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] develops a service plan for every client. The plan is developed with agency staff, the client or the client's representative or power of attorney, and family if the client wishes (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(e)). The plan covers ADL and in-home support; medication reminders, including frequency and time of day; treatments the client is receiving; activity; diet; functional limitations and essential procedures; mental health status; frequency of visits; equipment; and client limitations. The plan may not include tasks outside the worker scope in 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.40(c)(4). No physician signature is required. The plan is reviewed and revised as needed, and at least annually (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(g)), and is kept in the client record (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(h)).

definitions.definition: The written plan that describes the non-medical services a client will receive, how often, and the client-specific information a worker needs to provide them safely.
Steps a worker must follow to meet a client's specific functional limitations safely, such as how the client transfers or the client's emergency contact process.
A scheduled or event-triggered check of whether the plan still fits the client's needs and preferences, resulting in documented confirmation or revision.

procedures: The Home Services Supervisor drafts the plan from the assessment (SVC-02) during or immediately after the in-home visit and always before the first worker visit.
The supervisor reviews the draft with the client or representative or power of attorney and, if the client wishes, family. The client's wishes and preferences are written into the plan.
The plan lists ADL and in-home support tasks, such as bathing, dressing, meals, housekeeping, laundry and shopping, with the expected frequency and detail.

The plan states medication reminders, including how often and at what time of day, and confirms that medications are pre-selected by the client, a family member, a nurse or a pharmacist and are in containers other than prescription bottles (see SVC-05). It does not include medication setup.

The plan records treatments the client is receiving from others (for example, home health nursing), activity level, diet and any dietary limits, in terms of what the worker needs to know, not instructions for medical care.

The plan lists functional limitations and the essential procedures a worker must follow, mental health status, and any communication needs or cognitive issues, referencing SVC-12 for dementia clients.

The plan states the days, times and length of visits, and any equipment in the home or that the worker will use, such as walkers, lifts or shower chairs. The plan also lists client limitations, including any known hazards or safety risks.

The supervisor checks each task against the permitted tasks in 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.40(c)(4) and removes any out-of-scope task (see SVC-01). For conditioned tasks, the supervisor attaches the documentation of worker training and competency evaluation (see SVC-11).

The client or representative signs and dates the plan. The agency gives a copy to the client or representative and places the original in the client record. No physician signature is requested or required.
The supervisor gives each assigned worker a copy of the plan, or electronic access, and reviews tasks and essential procedures with the worker before the first visit. The worker acknowledges receipt.
Workers report to the supervisor the same day when the plan no longer fits, for example if the client declines a task, new limitations appear or equipment is missing.

The supervisor revises the plan whenever the client's condition, needs, preferences, hospitalization, schedule or payer authorization changes, and no later than 5 business days after learning of the change. Each revision is reviewed with the client or representative and signed.
At least every 12 months, and sooner if needed, the supervisor reassesses the client in the home and reviews the full plan. The review date and findings are documented, even if no changes are made.

For CCP and HSP clients, the supervisor compares the plan to program authorizations and informs the Care Coordination Unit or DHS-DRS counselor of changes that affect authorized hours or services (see SVC-10).
The Agency Manager audits a sample of plans each quarter for required content, scope compliance, signatures and annual review dates and reports results to the Quality Improvement committee (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures every client has a current plan, reviews audit results and corrects deficiencies.
Develops, reviews and revises plans with clients and families, ensures scope compliance and schedules annual reviews.
Follow the plan, review it before the first visit and report needed changes promptly.
Take part in plan development, share preferences and tell the agency about changes in needs.

documentation: Signed service plan in the client record with all required content
Documentation that the client or representative and, if wished, family took part
Revisions with dates and signatures
Annual review documentation
Worker acknowledgment of plan review
Task condition records for conditioned tasks
Quarterly plan audit results

policies.title: Supervision of Home Services Workers and Supervisory Visits
policies.applies_to: Agency Manager, Home Services Supervisors, trainers and all home services workers
policies.purpose: To make sure every home services worker is supervised by a qualified supervisor who is available at all times, that supervisory visits are made on schedule and when concerns arise, and that each worker is observed giving care at least annually.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] designates a supervisor who is available to workers for questions at all times (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.40(c)(6)). The supervisor makes supervisory visits to clients' homes. When an area of concern is noted, the supervisor makes an on-site visit to observe the worker giving care no later than the next supervisory visit. The supervisor also makes an annual on-site visit to observe and assess each worker giving care. As an agency standard, routine supervisory visits are made at least every 90 days, and more often if the client's condition, the service plan or a concern requires it. Supervisors and trainers meet the qualifications in 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.71(g) and are available to workers for continuing education (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.71(h)). This policy is part of the supervisory-visit policies submitted with the IDPH home services application (Form 445104).

definitions.definition: A person who meets the qualification requirements of 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.71(g) and who provides ongoing supervision of home services workers.
A visit by the supervisor to the client's home to review the client's satisfaction and needs, the service plan and the worker's performance.
A problem noticed through a visit, call, complaint, record review or report that could affect client safety, quality of care or compliance, for example a missed task or unsafe practice.
An on-site visit at least once a year during which the supervisor watches the worker give care to a client and assesses the worker's performance.

procedures: The governing body or Agency Manager designates in writing at least one qualified Home Services Supervisor and a backup, and posts their names and phone numbers where workers can reach them at any hour, including nights, weekends and holidays (see GOV-06).

The Agency Manager verifies each supervisor's and trainer's qualifications before assignment: either at least 2 years of qualifying experience within the last 5 years, or a current supervisory or trainer position plus training within the past year on the permitted tasks, provided or developed by a qualified professional. Evidence is filed in the personnel record (see PER-09).
The supervisor or backup answers worker questions at all times. After-hours calls are logged with the date, time, worker, client, question, advice given and any follow-up.
The supervisor schedules routine supervisory visits for each client at least every 90 days, tracks due dates on a supervision calendar and reviews the calendar weekly with the Agency Manager.

At each supervisory visit, the supervisor talks with the client or representative, reviews the service plan for accuracy, checks the visit documentation, asks about satisfaction and any concerns, and looks at the safety of the home and equipment.

The supervisor completes the supervisory visit form, which records the date, client, worker if observed, findings, plan changes needed, concerns and follow-up actions. The client or representative is offered the chance to sign.
When an area of concern is identified, the supervisor records it in the client record and notifies the Agency Manager within 1 business day.

For any area of concern about a worker's performance, the supervisor makes an on-site visit to observe the worker giving care no later than the next supervisory visit, and sooner when client safety is at risk. The visit is documented, including whether the concern was resolved.
Concerns about abuse, neglect or exploitation are handled immediately under SAF-01 and are not deferred to a supervisory visit.

At least once every 12 months, the supervisor makes an on-site visit to observe and assess each worker giving care to a client, using the competency checklist for the tasks on the plan. The observation is recorded and signed by the supervisor and the worker.

If an observation shows a performance gap, the supervisor gives immediate coaching, arranges retraining and a repeat competency evaluation, and documents the plan and completion date. Workers do not perform a task until competency is shown.
The supervisor reviews worker visit documentation and EVV records at least monthly for missed tasks, late arrivals and out-of-scope work, and addresses concerns with the worker (see SVC-07).

Supervisors and trainers are available to workers for continuing education, and training they provide is documented with date, minutes per topic, instructor and qualifications, content description and worker signature or electronic certificate with date and time stamp (see PER-03).
Supervisory visit findings go into each worker's personnel record for use in annual performance evaluations (see PER-08).

The Agency Manager reviews supervision calendars, overdue visits and annual observations each month, and reports timeliness and trends to the Quality Improvement committee (GOV-04). Any overdue visit is completed within 7 days of discovery and the cause is corrected.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures qualified supervisors are designated and adequate supervisory capacity is available.
Verifies supervisor qualifications, monitors the supervision calendar and ensures follow-up on concerns.
Is available to workers at all times, completes routine, concern-triggered and annual on-site visits, documents findings and coaches workers.
Call the supervisor with questions or concerns, take part in visits and complete retraining when assigned.

documentation: Written designation of supervisors and backup with qualification evidence
After-hours supervisor call log
Supervision calendar showing visit due dates and completion
Supervisory visit forms for each visit
Documentation of on-site visits following areas of concern
Annual on-site observation and assessment for each worker
Retraining and competency re-evaluation records
Monthly supervision review and Quality Improvement reports

policies.title: Medication Reminding (No Medication Setup)
policies.applies_to: All home services workers, supervisors and the Agency Manager
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] home services workers provide only the non-medical medication reminding that Illinois allows, and never perform medication setup or administration.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] workers may remind a client to take medications only when the medications were pre-selected by the client, a family member, a nurse or a pharmacist, and are stored in a container other than the original prescription bottle, such as a medication minder. Workers may not perform or provide medication setup, and may not administer, open or pour medications. Each client's service plan states the reminder frequency and time of day. Medication reminding is part of every worker's required initial training, and a worker may not remind a client of medications until trained. Missed doses, refusals and reactions are reported to the supervisor and the client's emergency contact.

definitions.definition: A verbal or similar prompt telling a client that it is time to take medications that were already selected and placed in an appropriate container by someone other than the worker.
Selecting, sorting, counting, pouring or placing medications into a minder or other container. Workers may not do this.
A container, such as a day-and-time pill organizer, filled by the client, a family member, a nurse or a pharmacist.
The person named in the client record to be notified of changes or emergencies.

procedures: At intake, the supervisor asks the client or representative whether medication reminders are wanted and records who selects and fills the client's medications (client, family member, nurse or pharmacist).

The supervisor confirms the medications are in a container other than a prescription bottle, such as a medication minder. If they are only in prescription bottles, the supervisor tells the client or representative that workers cannot remind from them. The supervisor documents the discussion and asks the client to arrange for a minder to be filled by the client, a family member, a nurse or a pharmacist.
The service plan (SVC-03) records the medication reminder frequency and time of day for each reminder. The plan does not include any task of setting up, opening, pouring or administering medications.
Before any worker gives medication reminders, the supervisor verifies that the worker has completed initial training that includes medication reminding and has been competency-evaluated (PER-03).
At each visit with a reminder scheduled, the worker reminds the client at the time stated in the plan, using words such as 'It is time for your medication.'
The worker may not open the minder compartment, pour or handle pills, or hand the client pills. The worker does not decide which medication or dose the client takes.

If a minder compartment appears empty, wrong or unfilled, the worker does not fill it. The worker calls the supervisor right away, and the supervisor contacts the client's emergency contact or the person who fills the minder.

If a client refuses a medication, the worker does not argue or force it. The worker records the refusal and calls the supervisor the same day, or immediately if the medication is critical or the client seems unwell.
If a client reports or shows a reaction, such as a rash, trouble breathing, confusion or a fall, the worker follows SVC-08, calls 911 for an emergency, and then calls the supervisor.
The supervisor notifies the client's emergency contact of missed doses, refusals and reactions on the day of the report, and documents the call in the client record.
The worker documents in the visit note that a reminder was given, the time, and the client's response, including any missed dose or refusal.

If a worker is asked by a client, family member or anyone else to set up, open or pour medications, the worker declines politely and tells the supervisor. The supervisor reminds the requester of the limit and documents the contact.
The supervisor reviews medication reminder documentation during supervisory visits (SVC-04) and at each service plan review.

A worker who performs medication setup or administration is removed from the assignment pending review under PER-07. The Agency Manager decides on corrective action and reports it to the QI program (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures this policy is followed, that medication reminding is included in initial training, and that violations are corrected.
Confirms medication containers at intake, writes the reminder schedule into the service plan, checks worker training, follows up on reports, and notifies emergency contacts.
Gives reminders only as the plan states, never sets up or administers medications, and reports and documents missed doses, refusals and reactions.
Arranges for medications to be selected and placed in a minder by the client, a family member, a nurse or a pharmacist.

documentation: Service plan entry showing reminder frequency and time of day
Intake note on who fills the medication container and the container type
Worker training record showing medication reminding completed
Visit notes documenting each reminder, missed dose or refusal
Notification to emergency contact and supervisor follow-up note
Supervisory visit notes

policies.title: Scheduling, Missed Visits and Continuity of Care
policies.applies_to: Scheduler, supervisors, home services workers and the Agency Manager
policies.purpose: To make sure clients receive scheduled visits at the frequency in their service plan, that missed visits are handled promptly and safely, and that care continues when a worker is unavailable.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] schedules visits at the frequency stated in each client's service plan and documents each service at each visit in the client record. Part 245 does not set a staffing ratio, visit minimum or missed-visit rule for home services agencies, so this policy sets the agency's own notification and replacement procedure. The agency will make every reasonable effort to staff each visit. When a visit cannot be staffed, it notifies the client promptly, arranges a replacement or reschedule, and escalates any safety concern. The agency's operating-hours policy tells clients how to reach the agency outside business hours.

definitions.definition: A visit at the day, time and duration agreed with the client and consistent with the visit frequency in the service plan.
A scheduled visit that does not occur, or that starts so late that the client's needs cannot be met as planned.
Keeping services going without gaps through assignment of familiar workers and orderly replacement or rescheduling.
A qualified, trained worker who covers a visit for the assigned worker.

procedures: The scheduler builds each client's schedule from the visit frequency in the current service plan (SVC-03) and the days and times agreed with the client or representative.
The scheduler assigns only workers who have completed required orientation, training, competency evaluation and background checks for the tasks in the client's plan (PER-02, PER-03).
Where possible, the scheduler assigns a regular worker and a named back-up worker to each client.
The scheduler gives each worker the assignment, the service plan tasks, the client's address and emergency contact, and the instructions for reporting problems.

A worker who cannot work a scheduled visit calls the scheduler or on-call supervisor as soon as the problem is known and, whenever possible, at least [NUMBER] hours before the visit. The worker does not arrange the replacement alone.
If a worker is late by more than 15 minutes, the worker calls the agency. The scheduler contacts the client and gives an estimated arrival time or arranges a replacement.
If a worker does not arrive and has not called, the scheduler tries to reach the worker within 30 minutes of the start time and calls the client to tell them.
The scheduler offers the client a replacement worker, a later time that day, or a reschedule, and records the client's choice.

If the client is believed to be alone with urgent needs, such as dementia, fall risk or a critical need for assistance, the supervisor treats the missed visit as urgent. The supervisor arranges immediate coverage or a welfare contact with the client's emergency contact, and follows SVC-08 if the client cannot be reached or seems at risk.
If a worker arrives and the client does not answer, the worker calls the supervisor. The supervisor tries the client and emergency contact, and follows SVC-08 if there is concern for safety.
The scheduler documents each missed, late or rescheduled visit, the reason, who was notified, the time of notification, and the replacement or reschedule.

The supervisor reviews a client's missed-visit pattern each week. If a client has repeated missed visits or a worker has repeated absences, the supervisor documents the trend and takes corrective action, including adjusting the schedule or assigning other workers.
Clients receive the agency's telephone number and the after-hours access instructions required by the operating-hours policy (GOV-06) with their service agreement, and again whenever they change.

The scheduler tells the client when a regular worker is being changed on a lasting basis, introduces the new worker where possible, and ensures the new worker is briefed on the service plan before the first visit.
The Agency Manager reviews missed-visit and late-visit data quarterly and reports results to the QI program (GOV-04).
Each worker documents the services provided at each visit, with the arrival and departure times, in the client record (SVC-07, REC-01).

responsibilities.duty: Builds schedules from service plans, assigns qualified workers, arranges replacements and records missed visits and client notifications.
Handles urgent missed visits, reviews patterns and takes corrective action.
Arrives on time, notifies the agency promptly of any absence or delay, and documents each visit.
Ensures sufficient staffing, keeps after-hours access available and reports missed-visit trends to QI.

documentation: Client schedules and assignments
Missed or late visit log with reason, notifications and replacement
Worker visit documentation for each visit
Client notification records
Weekly supervisor review notes and quarterly QI report

policies.title: Electronic Visit Verification and Timekeeping
policies.applies_to: Schedulers, billing staff, supervisors, home services workers and the Agency Manager
policies.purpose: To make sure visits are accurately verified and recorded, that Medicaid-funded personal care meets Illinois EVV requirements, and that worker hours are recorded accurately for payroll and billing.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] records the actual start time, end time and services of every visit. For Medicaid-funded personal care (IDoA CCP or DHS-DRS HSP), the agency uses electronic visit verification (EVV) as the state requires. Private-pay visits are outside the state EVV mandate but are still timed and documented under this policy. Worker documentation of each visit remains required in the client record even when EVV is used. The agency reviews EVV exceptions weekly and does not bill a Medicaid visit that lacks a matching EVV record.

definitions.definition: Electronic visit verification, a system that electronically captures information about a Medicaid-funded personal care visit.
The system into which Illinois integrates personal care and home health EVV data from March 2, 2026.
A visit record that is missing, incomplete or does not match the schedule or claim, such as a missing clock-in or clock-out.
The share of Medicaid visits with valid EVV records. HFS requires at least 75% quarterly compliance from April 1, 2026.

procedures: Before the agency serves any Medicaid-funded client, the Agency Manager confirms with HFS and the funding program the current EVV requirements and the system the agency must use, including the free state EVV solution, and records the decision.
The Agency Manager assigns an EVV administrator and sets up user accounts for schedulers, billing staff and workers who will use the system.

EVV elements are confirmed against current HFS documents. A vendor summary lists them as caregiver, member, service, time in, time out and GPS location, and the agency configures its process to capture whatever HFS requires.
Orientation (PER-03) trains each worker on the system and the clock-in and clock-out steps before the worker's first Medicaid-funded visit.

Each worker clocks in at the start of every Medicaid-funded visit and clocks out at the end, at the client's home, using the approved method. Workers may not clock in or out for another person or from a place other than the client's home unless the supervisor has approved a documented exception.
For private-pay visits, workers record start and end time on the agency's timekeeping form or system at the visit.

If a worker cannot use the system, such as a device failure or lost service, the worker calls the scheduler during the visit and records the actual times and the reason. The scheduler enters a manual edit with a stated reason code in the system.
Workers complete a visit note listing the services performed at every visit, for all clients regardless of payer, and sign or electronically submit it (REC-01).
The EVV administrator reviews EVV exceptions at least weekly. Each exception is corrected with documented support, such as a worker statement or schedule record, or the visit is not billed.

Manual edits require a reason and the approver's name. Supervisors review the rate of manual edits monthly. A pattern of edits for one worker or client is investigated for possible falsification (GOV-05).
Billing staff match each Medicaid claim to a valid EVV visit before submission. A claim without a matching EVV visit is held until the record is resolved, because it may deny.

The EVV administrator calculates the quarterly EVV compliance rate, compares it to the 75% HFS requirement, and reports it to the Agency Manager and the QI program (GOV-04). A rate below target triggers a written corrective plan.
Payroll uses actual recorded hours, including time worked, and complies with wage and hour rules (PER-06). Time records are kept under the retention requirements in REC-01.
Staff who falsify or knowingly submit inaccurate time or EVV records are subject to discipline up to termination and the matter is handled under GOV-05.

responsibilities.duty: Confirms current EVV requirements, assigns the EVV administrator and ensures compliance targets are met.
Manages accounts, reviews exceptions weekly, approves manual edits and reports the compliance rate.
Resolve exceptions and bill only visits supported by EVV and visit documentation.
Clocks in and out accurately, documents each visit and reports system problems at once.

documentation: EVV requirement confirmation and system setup record
Worker EVV training records
Visit notes for every visit
Manual edit log with reasons and approvals
Weekly exception review records
Quarterly EVV compliance report
Timekeeping and payroll records

policies.title: Change in Client Condition and Emergencies in the Home
policies.applies_to: All home services workers, supervisors and the Agency Manager
policies.purpose: To make sure workers observe and report changes in a client's condition, respond properly to emergencies, and that the agency follows up and documents.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] workers observe client functioning and report changes to the supervisor, the employer or a person the client designates. Workers are trained to recognize emergencies and start emergency procedures, including basic first aid and the client's emergency preparedness plan. Workers do not diagnose, give medical advice or perform medical care. In an emergency the worker calls 911 first. A crime in the home or a death other than by natural causes is reported to 911 and local law enforcement. Each client record contains an emergency contact, who is notified of significant changes and emergencies.

definitions.definition: Any noticeable change in the client's physical, mental or functional status, behavior, home environment or ability to manage daily activities.
A situation that threatens a client's life or health or requires immediate help, such as a fall with injury, chest pain, trouble breathing, unresponsiveness, fire or a crime.
The person listed in the client record to be notified of emergencies and significant changes.
The client's plan for responding to emergencies and disasters (SAF-04).

procedures: Orientation and annual training teach workers how to observe and report changes in client functioning, recognize emergencies, give basic first aid, and use the client's emergency preparedness plan (PER-03).

At every visit, the worker notes the client's general condition and any change from the baseline described in the service plan, such as mobility, appetite, mood, confusion, skin, or ability to do daily tasks.
The worker reports non-urgent changes to the supervisor by the end of the shift, or sooner if the change is significant. The worker records the change in the visit note.
If a worker finds open skin lesions while shampooing, the worker reports them to the agency and to the emergency contact as required.

In an emergency, the worker calls 911 right away, stays with the client if safe, and gives basic first aid within the worker's training. The worker does not move a seriously injured client unless there is immediate danger.
After calling 911, the worker calls the supervisor or on-call supervisor immediately, and the supervisor or worker notifies the client's emergency contact as soon as possible.
The worker follows the client's emergency preparedness plan for fires, severe weather, utility failure and similar events (SAF-04).
If a worker arrives and cannot find or reach the client, or finds the client unresponsive, the worker calls 911 and then the supervisor.

For a crime in the home, a death other than by disease or natural causes, or any staff-inflicted injury or sexual abuse, the worker or supervisor calls 911 and local law enforcement at once (SAF-07), and the supervisor starts the abuse reporting process (SAF-01).
If the worker suspects abuse, neglect or financial exploitation, the worker reports to the supervisor and follows SAF-01, which also covers the worker's own duty to report.
The worker does not give medications, treat symptoms or advise on medical matters. The worker may help the client call the client's own physician or may relay the change to the supervisor.

The supervisor, within one business day, reviews each reported change, contacts the client or family if needed, decides whether a service plan update or a nursing or medical referral is needed (SVC-03), and may arrange an extra supervisory visit.
If a client's needs have become medical or exceed the worker scope, the supervisor follows SVC-09.
The worker and supervisor document the event, time, persons contacted and outcome in the client record, and complete an incident report where required (SAF-02).

The supervisor reports the event to the Agency Manager the same day for any emergency, hospitalization, death or law enforcement contact, and the manager determines whether any state report is required (REC-02).

responsibilities.duty: Observes and reports changes, calls 911 in an emergency, gives only basic first aid, and documents.
Responds to reports, notifies emergency contacts, decides on follow-up and updates the service plan.
Reviews emergencies, ensures reporting and law enforcement notification, and reports to QI.

documentation: Visit notes on observations and changes
Incident report (SAF-02)
Emergency contact notification record
Supervisor follow-up note and service plan changes
Law enforcement or abuse report records, where applicable

policies.title: Discharge, Transfer and Discontinuation of Services
policies.applies_to: Agency Manager, supervisors, schedulers and home services workers
policies.purpose: To make sure services end only for proper reasons, with the notice Illinois requires, and that clients are helped to transition safely.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] follows this written discharge policy. Before terminating services, the agency gives the client at least 7 working days' written notice that states the reason, and keeps a copy in the client record. The 7-day notice does not apply when worker safety is at risk, and the risk is documented in the record.
