If a client's needs become medical, the agency refers the client to a home health or home nursing agency. The agency does not discharge a client on the basis of any protected class under 775 ILCS 5/1-103(Q). The service agreement states the conditions for termination.

definitions.definition: Ending services by the agency's decision.
Ending services for any reason, including client choice, relocation, hospitalization, death or loss of payment.
Days the agency's office is regularly open for business.
Referral or move of a client to another provider or level of care.

procedures: Only the Agency Manager, or the designated person acting in the manager's absence, may approve a discharge by the agency.

Acceptable reasons for agency-initiated discharge include: the client's needs have become medical or exceed the non-medical scope; the agency cannot safely meet the needs; non-payment after notice, under the service agreement; the client's request; a threat to worker safety; or agency closure. A reason based on a protected class is never acceptable.

Before discharge for medical needs, the supervisor documents the change in needs, consults the client or representative, and gives referral information for a home health or home nursing agency, or for other appropriate care.
The supervisor reviews the situation with the client or representative and tries to resolve the problem, where this is safe, before issuing notice.

The Agency Manager sends a written notice at least 7 working days before the last day of service. The notice states the reason, the last date of service, and referral or transition information. A copy goes to the client, the representative and any POA, and a copy goes in the client record.
If the client is a Medicaid participant, the supervisor also notifies the Care Coordination Unit or DHS-DRS contact as the program requires (SVC-10).
The agency continues providing scheduled services through the notice period unless the client declines.

The 7-day notice does not apply when worker safety is at risk, such as threats, violence, harassment or hazardous conditions. In that case, the Agency Manager may stop service immediately, documents in the record what happened and why the worker was at risk, and gives written notice as soon as possible.
If the safety risk involves a crime or injury, the agency follows SAF-07 and SAF-05.
If the client asks to stop services, the supervisor confirms the request, documents the date and reason, and offers transition help.

The supervisor arranges transition: it gives the client or representative a list of alternative providers where appropriate, and with the client's written authorization shares needed information with the new provider (CR-03, REC-03).

On the last day of service, the supervisor completes a discharge summary showing the reason, the date, the notice given and the client's status, and collects agency property and returns the client's property (CR-04).
For discharge due to hospitalization, death or relocation, the supervisor documents the date the agency learned of it and closes the record.
The agency retains the closed record under REC-01 and removes the client from the schedule and EVV or billing systems.
The Agency Manager reviews all agency-initiated discharges quarterly for compliance with notice rules and for non-discrimination, and reports to QI (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Approves agency-initiated discharges, signs notices, and ensures notice rules and non-discrimination are followed.
Assesses the situation, documents the reason, arranges referrals and transition and prepares the discharge summary.
Maintains scheduled services through the notice period and closes the schedule.

documentation: Written discharge notice with reason, date sent and recipients
Documentation of worker safety risk, where notice was shortened
Referral or transition information given
Discharge summary
Client request to discontinue, where applicable
Quarterly discharge review

policies.title: Coordination with Medicaid Programs (CCP, HSP) and Payers
policies.applies_to: Agency Manager, intake staff, billing staff and supervisors
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] accurately describes how it serves private-pay and Medicaid-program clients, coordinates correctly with state programs, and does not bill any program without confirmed authority.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is licensed by IDPH as a home services agency. A licensed home services agency serves private-pay or private-insurance clients. Medicaid clients are served through the IDoA Community Care Program (CCP) or the DHS-DRS Home Services Program (HSP). IDoA is the operating agency for the Persons who are Elderly waiver and HFS is the state Medicaid agency. The agency does not accept or bill a program referral until the Agency Manager has confirmed in writing the agency's enrollment and authority with that program. The agency follows each program's service authorization, service plan and EVV requirements and does not bill a program for services it did not provide or that were not authorized.

definitions.definition: The IDoA Community Care Program. Care Coordination Units assess and refer clients, and IDoA sets CCP in-home rates.
The DHS-DRS Home Services Program, serving people with severe disabilities under age 60.
The local entity that assesses CCP clients and refers them to in-home providers.
Services paid by the client, family or private insurance, outside Medicaid programs.

procedures: The Agency Manager states in the agency's marketing and intake materials that the agency is IDPH-licensed and describes accurately which payers it accepts (GOV-02).

The Agency Manager confirms the current enrollment and authorization steps with IDoA for CCP and with DHS-DRS for HSP, including whether a new agency can bill HSP at agency rates. These steps were not confirmed when this policy was written. The manager documents the date, the person contacted and the answer.

Programs that serve clients exclusively through CCP, DHS Office of Rehabilitation Services or the VA are not home services agencies. The Agency Manager reviews IDPH licensing rules with counsel before the agency accepts any change in its business model.

Until enrollment with a program is confirmed in writing, intake staff do not accept referrals from that program and refer callers to the correct program contact. Clients who want to apply for CCP are referred to the Senior HelpLine, 1-800-252-8966, which handles client applications, not provider enrollment.
Once enrolled, intake staff accept a referral only after receiving the program's authorization showing the services, hours and effective dates, and a copy goes in the client record.
The supervisor develops the agency service plan (SVC-03) consistent with the program's assessment and authorization. The plan may not include tasks outside the worker scope (SVC-01).

The agency delivers only the authorized services and hours. If a client needs more or different services, the supervisor contacts the CCU or DHS-DRS contact to request a change and does not bill for unauthorized hours.

Billing staff use only the current published program rates, as the reference points. The CCP in-home service (S5130) rate is $30.80 per hour, or $32.57 per hour with insurance, effective 1/1/2026. HSP maximum unit prices, updated 7/1/2026, are homemaker (4100) $30.80 per hour, personal assistant (4150) $20.00 per hour and non-agency CNA (4198) $23.00 per hour. Billing staff check current rate schedules at least quarterly and when rates are updated.
Medicaid-funded personal care visits are verified through EVV (SVC-07). Billing staff submit claims only for visits that have valid EVV and visit documentation.

The supervisor tells the CCU or the DHS-DRS contact about significant changes in the client's condition, hospitalization, missed visits that affect care, and any discharge, within the timeframes the program sets (SVC-08, SVC-09).
The agency keeps separate written billing procedures for each payer, and for private pay follows CR-06 on rates and billing disclosure.
The agency does not charge a program participant for a service the program pays for, and does not request payment from the client beyond what the program allows.
Billing staff and the Agency Manager follow the compliance rules in GOV-05, including accurate claims, overpayment refund, and prohibited kickbacks.
The Agency Manager keeps program contact information, authorizations, rate schedules and communications, and reviews payer requirements quarterly.
The Agency Manager notifies IDPH within 10 days of any change to the agency's information, using the Facility Information Change Form, and obtains IDPH approval before serving a new county (GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Confirms enrollment and authority with CCP and HSP before accepting referrals, and oversees billing integrity.
Accept only authorized referrals, record authorizations and refer unconfirmed program callers to the program.
Aligns the service plan with authorization and reports changes to the CCU or DHS-DRS contact.
Bill only authorized, verified services at current rates and keep payer records.

documentation: Written record of enrollment confirmation with IDoA and DHS-DRS
Program authorizations and referral records
Rate schedule reviews
Communications with CCU and DHS-DRS contacts
Payer-specific billing procedures
Claims and EVV support

policies.title: Task-Specific Conditions and Competency Evaluations (Bathing, Positioning, Feeding, Nail Care and Other Tasks)
policies.applies_to: All home services workers, Home Services Supervisors, trainers and the Agency Manager
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] home services workers perform personal care tasks only within the limits set by the Illinois Home Services Agency rules, and only after the required client feedback, worker training and agency competency evaluation are in place.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not assign a task listed in 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.40(c)(4) to a worker unless the conditions for that task are met and documented. For most tasks there are three conditions: (1) the client or the client's representative can give ongoing feedback to the worker; (2) the worker has been trained in the method; and (3) the agency has completed a competency evaluation of the worker. Some tasks also require an order from a health care professional. Bathing requires client-specific training and competency, and annual training and competency for all bathing types. Prescription shampoo requires an order and annual training. Nail filing for a client with circulatory or sensation problems requires a health care professional's order. Prescription compression devices require an order. Workers do not perform passive range of motion, do not trim nails, and do not provide skilled skin care. Feeding is limited to clients who can swallow independently and are upright; a client at high risk of choking must be served by a licensed home health or home nursing agency. Thickener may only be opened pre-measured under the client's direct observation, after training and competency. Positioning of a client who cannot signal for a change requires training and competency. Oxygen delivery support is assigned only to workers who are trained for clients on oxygen. A task that is not permitted, or whose conditions are not met, is not performed and is not placed on the service plan.

definitions.definition: A documented check, done by a qualified person designated by the Agency Manager, in which the worker shows the correct method for a task while being observed.
The client's or representative's ability to tell the worker during the task whether it is comfortable, correct or should stop.
A written or documented order from a licensed health care professional acting within their scope of practice, kept in the client record.
Training of the worker on the individual client's needs, equipment and preferred method, in addition to general task training.
Moving a client's limbs for them through a range of motion. Workers do not perform this task.

procedures: The Agency Manager designates in writing the persons qualified to train and perform competency evaluations (see PER-09). The designations are kept in the policy file.

At intake (SVC-02), the intake assessor records which personal care tasks the client needs and whether the client or representative can give ongoing feedback during each task. If the client cannot, the task is not added to the plan unless the rule permits it, and the Agency Manager is consulted.

Before a task is added to the service plan (SVC-03), the Home Services Supervisor checks the task against this policy and confirms that no health care professional's order is required, or that the order has been obtained and filed in the client record.

The Home Services Supervisor assigns the task only to a worker whose personnel file shows training in the method and a passed competency evaluation for that task. Where the task is client-specific, such as bathing, the file must also show client-specific training and competency.

Competency evaluations are done by direct observation of the worker performing the task on a person, or by return demonstration where observation of a client is not appropriate. The evaluator uses the agency's task checklist and records the date, task, result and evaluator signature.
A worker who does not pass is not assigned the task. The evaluator retrains the worker and repeats the evaluation. Retraining is documented.

Bathing: the supervisor confirms client-specific bathing training and competency for each bathing type (for example tub, shower, bed bath) before assignment. Annual training and a competency check on all bathing types are scheduled each year.
Prescription shampoo: the worker uses it only when a health care professional's order is in the record, the worker has been trained on the product, and annual training is current.

Nail care: workers may file nails but never trim or cut them. For a client with a circulatory or sensation problem, filing is done only with a health care professional's order in the record. When the client's condition is unknown, the worker does not file and reports to the supervisor.
Compression devices: workers apply a prescription compression device only with an order in the record and after training and competency evaluation.

Feeding and thickener: before assigning feeding, the supervisor confirms the client can swallow independently and can be upright. If a client shows coughing, choking or difficulty swallowing, the worker stops, follows SVC-08 and notifies the supervisor the same day. If the client is at high risk of choking, the agency refers the client to a licensed home health or home nursing agency (SVC-09). Thickener is used only when opened pre-measured, with the client directly observing, by a trained and evaluated worker.

Positioning: a worker positions a client who cannot signal for a change only after training and competency evaluation. The worker follows the position schedule on the service plan and reports skin changes to the supervisor. The worker performs no skilled skin care.

Oxygen: only workers assigned to clients on oxygen receive oxygen delivery training. Workers do not change stationary to portable oxygen unless the agency keeps an on-staff trained individual who can train and test workers, and the worker has passed that test. Otherwise the client or representative changes the supply.

Any other task under 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.40(c)(4) that is not named in this policy is handled the same way: the conditions are confirmed against the rule before the task is assigned, and the Agency Manager records the review.

Training and each competency evaluation are documented in the worker's personnel file (PER-05). The annual training record shows the ADL tasks and the oxygen delivery content for workers who serve clients on oxygen (PER-03).

The Home Services Supervisor reviews task assignments at each supervisory visit (SVC-04). A worker who is found doing an unauthorized task is stopped, the task is removed from assignment, and the event is reported to the Agency Manager as an incident (SAF-02).

The Agency Manager reviews this policy and the task checklists at least annually and when the rule changes (GOV-03). The Agency Manager also reads in full the remaining task items of 245.40(c)(4) before adding any of them to the agency's list of assignable tasks.

responsibilities.duty: Designates qualified trainers and evaluators, approves the list of assignable tasks, and reviews this policy annually.
Confirms conditions and orders before assigning tasks, matches tasks to evaluated workers, and checks compliance at supervisory visits.
Trains workers, performs and documents competency evaluations, and retrains workers who do not pass.
Performs only tasks for which training and competency are documented, stops and reports if conditions are not met.

documentation: Competency evaluation checklists signed by the evaluator, kept in the personnel file
Training records for each task, including client-specific bathing training
Health care professional's orders kept in the client record
Service plan task list showing conditions checked
Annual bathing and annual task training and competency records
Records of retraining and any unauthorized-task incidents

policies.title: Alzheimer's Disease and Related Dementias Services
policies.applies_to: All home services workers, Home Services Supervisors and the Agency Manager when serving or planning services for clients with dementia
policies.purpose: To ensure clients with Alzheimer's disease or a related dementia receive safe, respectful services from workers who understand dementia and are trained to respond to challenging behaviors.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides services to clients with dementia only with workers who have received the required training on understanding dementia and problem-solving for challenging dementia behaviors, which is part of initial training under 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.71(e). Each dementia client's service plan records the client's behaviors, triggers and safety needs, taken from the intake assessment. Workers communicate with clients with dementia in the manner taught in training. The agency will confirm the dementia-specific training hours and policy content required by the Department's dementia training standards and will keep its training program in line with them. No dementia training hour count is stated in this manual until that confirmation is complete.

definitions.definition: A decline in memory, thinking and function caused by Alzheimer's disease or a related condition that affects the client's daily life.
A behavior such as wandering, agitation, refusal of care, repeated questions or aggression that may place the client or others at risk or interferes with care.
A situation, time, setting or action that is known to bring on a challenging behavior.

procedures: During intake (SVC-02), the intake assessor asks the client, representative and referral source about any diagnosis of dementia, memory loss, wandering, confusion, agitation, refusal of care, sleep changes and past safety events. The answers are recorded in the assessment.

If dementia is indicated, the Home Services Supervisor reviews whether the agency can safely meet the client's needs with available trained workers before accepting the client. If not, the agency declines and refers (SVC-09).

The Home Services Supervisor writes the service plan (SVC-03) to include the client's known behaviors, triggers, calming approaches, communication preferences, wandering and home-safety needs, and who to call in a crisis.

The Agency Manager assigns only workers whose personnel file shows completion of the dementia content in initial training: understanding dementia, and problem-solving for challenging dementia behaviors.
Before the first visit, the Home Services Supervisor reviews the service plan with the worker, including the client's triggers and approaches that work.

Workers use the communication methods taught in training, such as a calm tone, short simple sentences, one step at a time, and allowing time to respond. They do not argue with, scold or restrain the client.

Workers do not use physical or chemical restraint. If a client's behavior puts the client or others in danger, the worker follows SVC-08, calls 911 if there is immediate danger, and notifies the supervisor right away.

Workers report new or worsening confusion, wandering, falls, refusal of care, or behaviors that are new for the client to the supervisor the same day, and document the observation in the visit record.

The supervisor follows up within one business day of a reported change, contacts the representative, and updates the service plan or refers the client to a physician or other professional as appropriate (SVC-08).

Any suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation of a client with dementia, including by a worker, is reported under SAF-01. Because a client with dementia may not be able to report for themselves, workers watch for signs and report on reasonable suspicion.
The supervisor evaluates each dementia client's plan at each supervisory visit (SVC-04) and whenever behaviors change.
Annual training for workers who serve dementia clients includes a refresher on the dementia and behavior topics, in addition to the required annual topics (PER-03).

The Agency Manager reviews the Department's dementia training standards and confirms in writing the required hours and content for the agency's training program before the agency accepts clients with dementia. The Agency Manager updates this policy and PER-03 to match and records the date of the review.
Complaints and incidents involving clients with dementia are included in the Quality Improvement review (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Confirms dementia training requirements, approves acceptance of dementia clients, and ensures only trained workers are assigned.
Builds behavior, trigger and safety information into the service plan, briefs workers, and reviews the plan at each supervisory visit.
Uses trained communication and de-escalation methods, protects the client's safety, and reports changes and concerns the same day.
Delivers and documents dementia content in initial and annual training.

documentation: Intake assessment noting dementia indicators
Service plan with behaviors, triggers and safety needs
Worker training records for dementia content
Visit notes of behavior changes and supervisor follow-up
Agency Manager's written confirmation of dementia training requirements

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, volunteers, contracted staff, supervisors and the Agency Manager
policies.purpose: To prevent abuse, neglect and financial exploitation of clients and to make sure every suspicion is reported, investigated and documented as required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.250 and the Adult Protective Services Act (320 ILCS 20).
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not tolerate abuse, neglect or financial exploitation of any client. On reasonable suspicion of abuse, neglect or financial exploitation of a client who is 60 or older, a client with a disability, or any eligible adult under the Adult Protective Services Act (320 ILCS 20), staff report to the elder abuse provider agency designated by the Illinois Department on Aging (IDoA) or to the Area Agency on Aging for the client's area. For a victim under 18, staff report to the DCFS Child Abuse Hotline. Employees and volunteers report to agency management and to the elder abuse provider agency or IDoA. Mandated-reporter duties under 320 ILCS 20 are not changed by this policy. If an employee is the alleged perpetrator, the employee is removed from direct client contact immediately and the allegation is investigated under SAF-08. Staff call 911 or local police immediately for staff-inflicted physical injury, sexual abuse by staff, a crime in the home by another person, or a death other than by disease or natural causes. The agency keeps a copy of each report on premises for 12 months. Every worker is trained on prevention and reporting at hire and each year. No employee is retaliated against for a good-faith report.

definitions.definition: Physical, sexual or emotional harm to a client, including hitting, rough handling, threats, humiliation, isolation and sexual contact of any kind.
Failure to provide, or to arrange for, care or goods and services the client needs to avoid physical or mental harm, whether by a caregiver or through self-neglect.
Improper use of a client's money, property or resources, including theft, misuse of accounts or cards, undue influence over gifts or documents, and taking payment for services not provided.
A belief, based on what a person sees, hears or is told, that abuse, neglect or exploitation may have occurred. Proof is not required before reporting.
An adult covered by the Adult Protective Services Act (320 ILCS 20), including adults with disabilities and adults age 60 or older, as defined in that Act.
The agency designated by IDoA, or the Area Agency on Aging, that receives reports and responds for the client's area.

procedures: At hire and before the first client assignment, each employee is trained on abuse, neglect and exploitation prevention and on the duty to report. The training is repeated every year as part of annual training (PER-03). Attendance and content are recorded in the personnel file.
Every employee signs an acknowledgment that they understand they must report, that failure to report may result in discipline, and that retaliation for reporting is prohibited.

The Agency Manager keeps a current contact list for the elder abuse provider agency or Area Agency on Aging for each county served, the IDoA Adult Protective Services line [IDoA ADULT PROTECTIVE SERVICES HOTLINE], and the DCFS Child Abuse Hotline [DCFS CHILD ABUSE HOTLINE]. The list is confirmed every six months and whenever a number changes, and is posted in the office and on the wallet card given to each worker.
A worker who sees or suspects abuse, neglect or exploitation, or who is told of it, first makes sure the client is safe. If anyone is in immediate danger, the worker calls 911.

The worker reports the suspicion immediately, and no later than the end of the shift, to the Home Services Supervisor or Agency Manager at [PHONE], and to the elder abuse provider agency or IDoA (or to the DCFS Child Abuse Hotline for a victim under 18). The worker does not wait for supervisor approval and does not investigate on their own.

For an event that requires an immediate call (staff-inflicted physical injury, sexual abuse by staff, a crime in the home by another person, or a death other than by disease or natural causes), staff call 911 or local police at once and then notify the Agency Manager. See SAF-07.
A person who receives a report from a worker confirms that the report to the designated agency has been made. If it has not, the supervisor or Agency Manager makes it the same day.

The person who made the report records what was seen or said, the date, time, persons involved, the agency contacted, the name of the person spoken to and the time of the report. The record is placed in the incident file, not shared with the alleged perpetrator.

If the alleged perpetrator is an employee, the Agency Manager removes that employee from all direct client contact immediately, arranges coverage for the client's visits, and starts the investigation under SAF-08. Removal is not disciplinary action and does not mean guilt.

If the alleged perpetrator is a family member or another person, the supervisor contacts the designated agency for guidance, develops a safety plan for the client and worker with the client's input, and updates the service plan (SVC-03).
The Agency Manager or designee completes a written investigation report within 14 days of the initial report, as described in SAF-08.

Within 24 hours after the investigation is completed, the Agency Manager sends the written report to the Illinois Department of Public Health, Home Services Program (IDPH, 217-782-7412 or DPH.COOS@illinois.gov) and keeps a copy for 12 months.
The Agency Manager keeps each report made to the designated agency, and each investigation report, on the agency's premises for at least 12 months from the date of the report.
The Agency Manager checks that the client's representative and any payer program (SVC-10) are informed of the report and outcome as required, keeping confidentiality under CR-03.
The Agency Manager reviews all reports quarterly for patterns, such as the same worker, client or location, and takes corrective action through the Quality Improvement program (GOV-04).
The agency uses a pre-hire background check and Health Care Worker Registry check (PER-02), supervisory visits (SVC-04) and client education on rights (CR-01) as prevention measures.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures reports are made, removes accused employees from client contact, completes the 14-day investigation, sends the report to IDPH within 24 hours of completion, and keeps records for 12 months.
Receives worker reports, confirms outside reports are made, protects the client, and monitors for signs at supervisory visits.
Report reasonable suspicion immediately, protect the client's safety, and cooperate with investigations.
Delivers and documents abuse and neglect training at hire and annually.

documentation: Training records on abuse, neglect and exploitation (hire and annual)
Employee acknowledgment of reporting duty
Copy of each report to the elder abuse provider agency, IDoA, DCFS or police, kept 12 months on premises
Written investigation report and IDPH transmittal record, kept 12 months
Record of removal from client contact and of return decisions
Quarterly report review notes

policies.title: Incident Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, supervisors and the Agency Manager
policies.purpose: To make sure every incident involving a client or worker is reported, reviewed and followed up, and that incidents that meet the reporting rules in 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.250 are sent to the right authority.
policies.policy: Part 245 does not contain a separate incident-reporting rule, so [AGENCY NAME] sets its own incident reporting system. The categories that require outside reporting under 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.250 are abuse, neglect, financial exploitation, staff-inflicted injury, sexual abuse, a crime in the home, and a death other than by disease or natural causes. These are handled under SAF-01, SAF-07 and SAF-08. In addition, the agency requires an internal incident report for client falls, client injuries, missing or damaged property, medication reminding errors, worker injuries, exposure to infectious disease, unsafe-home events and any other unusual event. A worker reports an incident to the supervisor immediately and submits a written incident report by the end of the shift, and no later than 24 hours after the event. The supervisor follows up and the Agency Manager reviews the incident.

definitions.definition: Any unusual event involving a client, worker or property that causes or could cause harm, loss or a complaint.
The agency's written form recording the facts of an incident, actions taken and follow-up.
A missed, late or wrong reminder, or any worker action beyond reminding, as defined in SVC-05.

procedures: The worker attends to the safety of the client and self first. If there is an emergency, the worker calls 911 and follows SVC-08.
The worker notifies the Home Services Supervisor by phone at [PHONE] immediately after the event. After hours, the worker uses the on-call number in GOV-06.

If the event is suspected abuse, neglect, financial exploitation, staff-inflicted injury, sexual abuse, a crime in the home or an unnatural death, the supervisor starts SAF-01 and SAF-07 steps at once and does not wait for the written incident report.

The worker completes the incident report form by the end of the shift and no later than 24 hours after the event. The form records the date, time, place, persons present, what happened in objective terms, the client's condition, who was notified and what was done.
The supervisor reviews the report within one business day, contacts the client or representative if not already notified, and records the contact.

The supervisor decides on follow-up, which may include a change to the service plan (SVC-03), additional worker training, a supervisory visit, a referral to a health care professional or a safety plan.
A worker injury is also referred for first aid or medical care and recorded for workers' compensation. Exposure to blood or infectious disease is handled under SAF-03 and PER-04.
Property loss or damage and any suspicion of theft are handled under CR-04, and the Agency Manager is notified the same day.
If the client is a Medicaid program participant, the supervisor checks whether the program requires notice of the incident and, if so, sends it under SVC-10.
The completed incident report is placed in an incident log. A copy or a summary is filed in the client record when it concerns care of that client.
The Agency Manager reviews each incident report, signs it and records the closing action. Incidents involving possible abuse or neglect are closed only when SAF-08 is completed.
The Agency Manager reviews all incidents each quarter for trends by type, worker, client and time, and reports results to the Quality Improvement program (GOV-04).
Incident reports are confidential and are released only as allowed by CR-03 and REC-03. Records are retained under REC-01.

responsibilities.duty: Secures safety, reports the incident immediately and completes the written report by end of shift or within 24 hours.
Reviews each report within one business day, notifies the representative, and carries out follow-up.
Closes each incident, ensures outside reports are made, and reviews incident trends quarterly.

documentation: Incident report forms
Incident log
Client record entries for incidents affecting care
Notes of notification to the client or representative and any payer
Quarterly incident trend review

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All employees, supervisors and the Agency Manager
federal: 29 CFR 1910.1030 (only where tasks create occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials)
policies.purpose: To prevent the spread of infection among clients and workers through written procedures for investigating, controlling and preventing infections, as required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.75(a).
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] develops and carries out written policies and procedures for investigating, controlling and preventing infections, and follows current CDC guidance on standard precautions and hand hygiene. All workers are trained on hygiene and infection control at hire and every year. Workers who show symptoms of a communicable disease, or who have been exposed, report to the supervisor and are removed from client contact until the conditions for return in PER-04 are met, as required by the employee health policy under 245.30(c)(1)(H). The influenza and pneumococcal vaccination duties in 245.55 apply to home health and home nursing agencies and not to home services agencies, so [AGENCY NAME] does not provide or arrange client vaccination. The agency performs an exposure determination under the OSHA bloodborne pathogens standard for any task, such as pericare, catheter bag emptying or ostomy bag emptying, that could expose a worker to blood or other potentially infectious materials.

definitions.definition: Basic infection control practices used with every client, including hand hygiene, gloves, cleaning and safe handling of soiled items.
Contact with blood, body fluids or a communicable disease in a way that could cause infection.
A written review of job tasks to identify which tasks could expose a worker to blood or other potentially infectious materials.
Items such as gloves, masks and aprons worn to protect against contact with infectious material.

procedures: The Agency Manager designates an infection control lead [INFECTION CONTROL LEAD NAME] who keeps current CDC guidance, updates these procedures and reports to the Agency Manager.

At hire and before the first client assignment, each worker receives training on hygiene and infection control, including hand hygiene, glove use, cleaning of the home environment, laundry, handling of soiled items and respiratory etiquette. The training is repeated each year (PER-03). It is documented in the personnel file.

Workers perform hand hygiene before and after client contact, before and after gloving, after toileting or pericare tasks, after handling soiled laundry or trash, and before food preparation or feeding.
The agency supplies gloves and other PPE at no cost to workers. Workers wear gloves for contact with body fluids, soiled items or broken skin, and change gloves between tasks and clients.

Workers do not report to work, and do not remain at a client's home, with symptoms such as fever, vomiting, diarrhea, a productive cough, an undiagnosed rash or draining skin lesion. They call the supervisor at [PHONE] as soon as they know, before the scheduled visit when possible.

A worker who reports symptoms or an exposure is removed from client contact. The supervisor records the report, arranges coverage for the client's visits (SVC-06), and follows PER-04 on evaluation and return to client contact.

A worker who learns a client has a communicable disease informs the supervisor at once. The supervisor reviews whether additional precautions are needed, shares only what is needed with workers under CR-03, and updates the service plan.

If a client shows signs of infection, such as fever, new cough, wound redness or drainage, or new confusion, the worker reports to the supervisor the same day. The supervisor contacts the client or representative and recommends medical follow-up (SVC-08). Workers do not give treatment.

Workers handle soiled linen, clothing and trash with gloves, bag them at the point of use and do not carry them against the body. Sharps found in a home are not touched; the worker tells the supervisor, who advises the client on safe disposal.

The Agency Manager performs a written exposure determination under 29 CFR 1910.1030 for each job category, reviews it each year and when tasks change. If any task creates occupational exposure, the agency follows the standard's training, PPE, exposure control plan, Hepatitis B vaccine offer and post-exposure evaluation duties for those workers.

After an exposure to blood or other potentially infectious material, the worker washes the area at once, reports to the supervisor immediately, and the Agency Manager arranges prompt medical evaluation at no cost to the worker. The event is recorded under SAF-02.

Each reported infection or suspected spread of infection among workers or clients is investigated by the infection control lead within three business days. The investigation records who was affected, likely source, contacts, actions taken and the outcome.
The Agency Manager reports to the local health department any reportable disease required by law and records the report. Additional reporting requirements are found in REC-02.
The Agency Manager reviews infection data each quarter as part of Quality Improvement (GOV-04) and corrects problems found.

The agency does not provide, require or document client influenza or pneumococcal vaccination, because these duties do not apply to this license type. Workers may give clients general public health information when asked.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains this policy, assigns an infection control lead, ensures PPE supply and the exposure determination, and arranges post-exposure care.
Keeps current CDC guidance, investigates infection events and reports to the Agency Manager.
Receives symptom and exposure reports, removes and returns workers according to PER-04, and arranges coverage.
Follows standard precautions, uses PPE, and reports symptoms and exposures promptly.

documentation: Infection control training records at hire and annually
Symptom and exposure reports and removal/return records
Infection investigation records
Written exposure determination and annual review
Post-exposure evaluation records (kept confidential)
Quarterly infection review in Quality Improvement minutes

policies.title: Client Emergency and Disaster Plans
policies.applies_to: All home services workers, Home Services Supervisors and the Agency Manager
policies.purpose: To ensure every client has an individual emergency plan, every worker is trained to carry it out, and [AGENCY NAME] can continue service to clients during severe weather, disasters and staff shortages.
policies.policy: At intake, [AGENCY NAME] helps each client or representative prepare a written emergency preparedness plan for the client. Workers are trained at hire to carry out the client's emergency plan, and every year on disaster procedures, as required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.71(e) and (f). Each client record contains an emergency contact (245.210(h)). The agency also keeps an agency continuity plan for severe weather and staff shortages. The agency is not required by the Part 245 sections reviewed to adopt an agency-wide emergency preparedness plan of the kind required of other provider types, and the federal home health emergency preparedness rule does not apply to this license; the agency adopts the continuity plan below as good practice.

definitions.definition: A written plan, specific to one client, telling the worker what to do in a fire, severe weather, power loss, medical emergency or other disaster.
Equipment the client relies on that needs electricity, such as oxygen concentrators, powered beds, lifts or nebulizers.
The agency's plan for keeping essential visits going when weather, disasters or staff shortages interfere.

procedures: During the intake assessment (SVC-02), the assessor asks about the client's ability to evacuate or shelter, mobility aids, medical equipment, power-dependent devices, oxygen, pets, hearing, vision and cognitive limits, nearby help, transportation and the nearest safe place.

The assessor writes the client emergency plan with the client or representative. The plan lists evacuation routes and ability, fire and severe weather shelter areas, power-dependent devices and back-up arrangements, the client's emergency contact, physician, pharmacy, and who the worker calls first.

The client or representative reviews and signs the plan. A copy stays in the client's home where workers can find it, and a copy is placed in the client record. The plan is part of the service plan review (SVC-03).

The emergency contact and the representative's contact information are confirmed at intake and checked at each supervisory visit and plan update (SVC-04). Changes are made in the record within one business day.
Before the first visit, the supervisor reviews the client's emergency plan with the worker. The worker confirms that they know exits, shelter places, equipment and the contacts.

At hire, each worker is trained to carry out the client's emergency plan, including first aid and emergency response, and every year on disaster procedures. Training is recorded in the personnel file (PER-03).

In a fire, medical emergency or immediate danger, the worker first calls 911, then helps the client to safety if the worker can do so without undue risk, and then calls the supervisor at [PHONE]. The worker does not move a client in a way they were not trained to do (SVC-08).
In severe weather or a disaster, the worker follows the client's plan, moves with the client to the shelter area if the plan says so, and contacts the supervisor when safe.

For a power loss, the worker checks power-dependent devices and starts the back-up arrangement in the plan, and calls 911 if the client's health is at risk. The worker notifies the supervisor and the client's emergency contact.

If a worker cannot reach a client's home, or a client cannot be found at the scheduled visit, the worker follows SVC-06 and SVC-08, including contacting the emergency contact and requesting a well-being check when the situation calls for it.

When a weather alert or local disaster is announced, the Home Services Supervisor reviews the schedule on the same day, identifies clients with the greatest need (for example those who depend on oxygen, are alone or are bed-bound) and calls them to review the plan and confirm that visits will go forward or be rescheduled.

If severe weather or staff shortage prevents a visit, the supervisor calls the client or representative before the scheduled time when possible, assigns a back-up worker, asks a family member or emergency contact to cover the gap, and records what was done (SVC-06).
The Agency Manager keeps a current list of workers by area, their availability and a back-up on-call roster, and ensures after-hours access under GOV-06.
After a disaster or emergency event, the supervisor contacts each affected client and worker, checks safety, restores service, and records the event as an incident (SAF-02).
The Agency Manager reviews this policy, the client plan form and the continuity plan every year, and after any activation, and records changes through document control (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the continuity plan and on-call roster and reviews this policy annually.
Ensures each client has a current emergency plan and contacts, briefs workers, and manages scheduling in severe weather.
Completes the client emergency plan with the client or representative at intake.
Knows and follows the client's emergency plan, calls 911 when needed and informs the supervisor.

documentation: Signed client emergency plan in the client record and in the home
Emergency contact and representative contact information in the client record
Worker training records on emergency plans and disaster procedures
Severe weather or staff shortage call logs and scheduling changes
Incident reports for emergencies and disasters
Annual review of the continuity plan

policies.title: Caregiver Safety in the Home and Workplace Violence
policies.applies_to: All home services workers, supervisors, the Agency Manager, intake staff and office staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To identify dangers to workers in clients' homes before services begin and while they continue, to protect workers from those dangers, and to prevent and respond to workplace violence. This policy meets the Illinois requirement for written procedures to identify and protect staff from dangers in the home, and it serves as the agency's employee health and safety policy for the IDPH application package.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will provide a workplace free of recognized hazards likely to cause death or serious physical harm. Before the first visit, the agency will complete a home safety check at intake, and it will repeat the check when conditions change. Workers will be trained on personal and environmental safety precautions. A worker may leave a home that is unsafe, and the agency will not penalize the worker for doing so in good faith. The agency will not continue services in a home where worker safety is at risk. Threats and acts of violence against workers, and by workers, are not tolerated. Each will be reported, documented and reviewed.

definitions.definition: A structured review done at intake and updated as needed. It covers hazards to the worker in the client's home and surroundings, including pets, firearms, smoking, bed bugs or other pests, unsafe physical conditions and the safety of other people in the home.

Any threat, harassment, intimidation, physical assault, sexual assault or other aggressive act directed at a worker by a client, family member, visitor or coworker, in the client's home or in the agency office.
A home where a worker reasonably believes there is an immediate risk of injury, illness, violence or serious hazard.
A situation in which continuing services would place a worker in danger. It is the basis for ending or suspending services without the usual advance notice.

procedures: The intake coordinator completes the Home Safety Check form during the initial assessment visit or call (see SVC-02). It records pets and how they are controlled, firearms and how they are stored, smoking and oxygen use, signs of bed bugs, roaches or other infestation, clutter and fall hazards, working smoke detectors, lighting, stairs, the neighborhood and parking, and any known history of aggression by the client or others in the home.

The coordinator asks the client or family to secure or confine pets during visits, to store firearms unloaded and locked, and to refrain from smoking during care or near oxygen. These requests are written into the service plan (see SVC-03).

The Agency Manager or supervisor reviews each completed Home Safety Check before the first visit. Where a hazard is found, the reviewer sets controls in writing, such as pet confinement, a two-person first visit, a change of work area, or a request to correct the condition. The reviewer then decides whether services can start safely.
Before the first assignment, the supervisor gives the worker a safety briefing on any hazards noted for that home and the controls to use. The worker signs that the briefing was received.

During orientation, and again each year, trainers teach basic personal and environmental safety precautions. These include recognizing and de-escalating aggressive behavior, safe lifting and body mechanics, trip and fall hazards, fire safety, safe use of equipment, and what to do in an emergency (see PER-03 and SAF-04).

Workers carry a charged mobile phone or have other reliable means to reach the office. They let the office know of any change in their schedule or location, and they follow the after-hours contact procedure in GOV-06.

A worker who feels unsafe may leave at any time. The worker should go to a safe location, call 911 first if there is immediate danger, and then call the office on-call supervisor without delay. The worker must not be disciplined for leaving a home in good faith because of a safety concern.

The supervisor documents every report of an unsafe home or threat on an Incident Report (see SAF-02) on the same day. The report states the specific risk, who was involved, what the worker saw or heard, and what was done.

The supervisor contacts the client or representative and checks the client's safety and need for care. If the client is at risk without services, the supervisor makes arrangements under SVC-08 and SVC-09 so that the client is not left without help. The supervisor also considers whether the situation requires a report under SAF-01 or a call to law enforcement under SAF-07.

If the hazard can be fixed (for example, a pet is confined, a firearm is secured, or a hazardous condition is repaired), the supervisor re-inspects the home and records the corrected condition before sending a worker back. If the hazard cannot be corrected, the Agency Manager decides whether to suspend or end services. Under the Illinois rule on termination of services, the advance written notice period for terminating a client does not apply where worker safety is at risk. The Agency Manager documents the specific risk that supports that decision, and follows SVC-09 for client notice and referral.

Threats or violence by a client or family member are reported to the supervisor immediately. The agency offers the affected worker support, medical attention if needed and time off, and may reassign the worker. Staff are advised to report a workplace injury to the Agency Manager on the day it occurs, so the agency can meet its workers' compensation obligations.

Threats or violence by a worker or other agency employee against a coworker or client are investigated under SAF-08 and SAF-01. The agency removes the employee from client contact while the matter is investigated.
The Agency Manager reviews all unsafe-home reports and workplace violence incidents at least quarterly, looks for trends, and reports the results to the Quality Improvement Program (see GOV-04).

Supervisors repeat the Home Safety Check at each supervisory visit (see SVC-04) and whenever a worker reports a new hazard, a new person or pet in the home, or a change in the client's behavior or health.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains this policy, makes final decisions to suspend or end services for worker safety, ensures retaliation against workers who report hazards does not occur, and reviews incidents quarterly.
Completes the Home Safety Check at intake and records requested controls.
Reviews safety checks, briefs workers, follows up on safety reports and re-inspects homes after corrections.
Follows safety precautions, reports hazards and threats immediately, and may leave an unsafe home and report it.
Responds to worker safety calls after hours and arranges immediate support.

documentation: Home Safety Check form in the client record
Worker safety briefing acknowledgment
Incident Reports for unsafe-home and workplace violence events
Documentation of risk supporting any suspension or ending of services for worker safety
Training records showing safety precaution topics (date, minutes, instructor and worker signature)
Quarterly review notes for the QI Program

policies.title: Transporting Clients
policies.applies_to: All home services workers, supervisors and management of [AGENCY NAME] who drive, or arrange transport for, clients
policies.purpose: To make sure that when a worker helps a client get to appointments or errands, the client is transported safely and lawfully and the agency has the insurance coverage it needs. The Illinois rules do not set transport-specific standards, so this policy sets the agency's own requirements.
policies.policy: Helping clients get to and from appointments and shopping is a permitted home services task, and [AGENCY NAME] offers it only when it is listed in the client's service plan and the agency's list of services. A worker may drive a client only if the worker holds a valid Illinois driver's license, the vehicle is insured, the client agrees, and the other conditions in this policy are met. The agency will confirm with its liability carrier that client transport, including use of workers' personal vehicles (hired and non-owned auto use), is covered before it offers transport. If coverage is not confirmed, the agency will not drive clients and will limit the service to accompanying clients who use other transport.

definitions.definition: A worker driving a client in a vehicle, whether the worker's own or the agency's, to an appointment, shopping, or other service listed in the service plan.
Liability coverage for vehicles the agency does not own, such as workers' personal cars used on agency business.
Fastening a wheelchair or other mobility device to a vehicle using devices designed for that purpose, with the client in a belted seat.

procedures: The Agency Manager contacts the liability insurance carrier before the agency offers transport. The Manager asks in writing whether client transport and hired and non-owned auto use are covered, and what limits and conditions apply. The written answer is kept with the insurance policy. The agency does not offer driving until coverage is confirmed.

The agency's list of services states whether transport is offered, with the scope of that service. It is given to every client before the contract, with the signed contract, and whenever it changes (see SVC-01 and CR-06).

During assessment, the intake coordinator decides whether the client can safely ride in a passenger car (can transfer, sit upright and use a seat belt) or needs a vehicle with a lift or ramp. If the agency cannot safely meet the client's transport needs, the coordinator tells the client and helps arrange other transport.
The service plan must list transport as a task, with destinations or types of trips, the client's mobility needs and any precautions (see SVC-03).

Before a worker is first assigned to drive, HR checks and copies the worker's valid driver's license and, for a personal vehicle, proof of current auto liability insurance. These go in the personnel file. HR re-checks both at least annually and when a license or policy expires.

The agency does not assign driving to a worker whose license is suspended, revoked or expired, or who lacks proof of insurance, or whose driving record the Agency Manager considers unsafe under the agency's written driving standard.
The client or representative gives informed consent to transport in writing before the first trip, either on the service agreement or a separate form. The client may refuse a ride at any time.

Before each trip, the worker confirms that the vehicle is in safe working order, including tires, lights and brakes. The worker makes sure the vehicle is clean and free of clutter and that the client is not placed in a front seat equipped with an active airbag when unsafe for the client.

Every passenger, including the worker, wears a seat belt. The worker does not start the vehicle until the client is belted. Workers do not drive while using a hand-held phone and do not smoke in the vehicle while a client is aboard.

A client who uses a wheelchair or other mobility device may be transported only in a vehicle designed for it and with securement devices the worker has been trained to use. A worker is not to lift a client who cannot transfer, or fold a client into a vehicle that is unsuitable. If the worker cannot do the task safely, the worker calls the supervisor.
Workers do not transport a client outside the scope of the service plan, do not carry other passengers during a client trip, and do not leave a client unattended in a vehicle.

The worker records each trip in the visit notes: date, start and end times, destination, mileage if applicable, and any problem during the trip. Mileage is not billed to the client unless the service agreement and rate disclosure say so (see CR-06).

If there is a crash, injury or illness during transport, the worker calls 911 if anyone needs medical help, then notifies the supervisor. The worker completes an Incident Report the same day (see SAF-02). The supervisor reports the loss to the insurance carrier as the policy requires, and follows SVC-08 for any change in the client's condition.
The supervisor reviews transport practices at supervisory visits and the Agency Manager reviews transport incidents each quarter in the QI Program (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Confirms insurance coverage in writing, approves the driving standard, and decides whether the agency offers transport.
Verifies and keeps driver's license and vehicle insurance for each driving worker and tracks renewals.
Confirms transport is in the service plan, checks securement training, and reviews trip records.
Drives only when eligible and authorized, uses seat belts and securement, and documents and reports trips and incidents.

documentation: Written carrier confirmation of transport and hired and non-owned auto coverage
Certificate of liability insurance
Copy of each driving worker's license and vehicle insurance, with review dates
Client transport consent
Service plan listing transport and mobility needs
Visit notes recording each trip
Incident Reports for crashes or injuries
Securement training records

policies.title: Law Enforcement Notification and Crime in the Client's Home
policies.applies_to: All employees, supervisors and management of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure staff protect clients, call police, fire, ambulance and rescue services without delay, protect a possible crime scene, and notify the proper authorities when abuse or a crime occurs. This is the written law-enforcement notification policy required under 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.250.
policies.policy: Client safety comes first. Staff will call 911 or local law enforcement immediately when (1) a staff member's physical abuse causes injury to a client, (2) a staff member sexually abuses a client, (3) a crime is committed in the client's home by another person, (4) a client dies other than by disease processes or natural causes, or (5) any allegation of physical abuse, sexual abuse or crime is reported to the agency. Calling police does not replace reporting to the elder abuse provider agency, IDoA or the Area Agency on Aging, the DCFS Child Abuse Hotline where a child is the victim, or the agency's own management. The agency will report to all required parties.

definitions.definition: Any criminal act in the client's residence by someone other than an agency employee, such as theft, burglary, assault, or a break-in, that the worker witnesses, discovers or is told about.
Steps taken to avoid disturbing evidence until police arrive and advise on what may be touched or cleaned.
The agency designated by IDoA to receive and respond to reports of abuse, neglect and financial exploitation of older adults and eligible adults.

procedures: Any worker who sees or learns of an emergency, a crime, a suspicious death or abuse first makes sure the client and himself or herself are safe. If danger continues, the worker leaves the area or home with the client if it is safe to do so.

The worker calls 911 immediately for the situations in the policy and requests police, fire, ambulance or rescue as needed. Workers do not wait to talk with a supervisor before calling 911 in an emergency.
The worker gives first aid within the limits of the worker's training and stays with the client until help arrives, unless leaving is necessary for safety (see SVC-08).

If a crime may have occurred, the worker does not move, clean or touch items in the area beyond what is needed to protect life. The worker does not allow others to disturb the scene, and asks the police dispatcher or responding officer what needs to be preserved.

After calling 911, the worker notifies the on-call supervisor or Agency Manager by phone as soon as possible, and no later than the end of the shift, at [PHONE]. The worker then gives a written statement.

The supervisor or Agency Manager confirms that police have been called. If they have not, the supervisor or Agency Manager calls. They also notify the client's representative or emergency contact, within the limits of the privacy requirements in CR-03.

If the allegation concerns abuse, neglect or exploitation, the Agency Manager or designee also reports to the elder abuse provider agency or IDoA, or the DCFS Child Abuse Hotline for a victim under 18, under SAF-01. Police notification does not satisfy this duty. Mandated-reporter duties under the Adult Protective Services Act continue regardless.
If the alleged offender is an employee, the Agency Manager removes the employee from client contact right away and begins the investigation and 14-day written report under SAF-08.

If the client dies other than from disease or natural causes, the worker calls 911, stays at the scene as police direct, and does not disturb the scene. The Agency Manager notifies the family or representative as directed by police and the appropriate authorities.

The agency cooperates with law enforcement and gives police the information they request, within applicable law. The Agency Manager decides who speaks for the agency and logs each contact with law enforcement.

The worker or supervisor completes an Incident Report the same day (see SAF-02). It states the time police were called, the responding agency, officer names and report number if provided, and actions taken to protect the client.
The Agency Manager follows up with the client and reviews the service plan, the home safety check and any need for added precautions or a change in services (see SVC-03 and SAF-05).
Each year, the agency trains workers on this policy, including how to call for help, how to preserve a scene, and that police notification is separate from agency reporting (see PER-03).
The Agency Manager reviews each law-enforcement notification in the QI Program for timeliness and completeness (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures police and all required agencies are notified, directs removal of accused employees, and keeps records.
Takes worker reports after hours, confirms 911 has been called and starts the notifications.
Calls 911 immediately in the listed situations, protects the scene, and reports to the supervisor.
Report any allegation or suspicion of abuse or crime to management and to the proper agencies.

documentation: Incident Report with police agency, time called and report number
Worker written statement
Log of law-enforcement contacts
Record of reports to the elder abuse provider agency, IDoA or DCFS (kept on premises 12 months)
Training records covering this policy

policies.title: Investigation of Allegations Against Employees and 14-Day Written Report
policies.applies_to: The Agency Manager, supervisors, investigators and all employees of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure every allegation that an employee abused, neglected or financially exploited a client is acted on at once, that the client is protected, and that a complete written investigation report is done within 14 days and sent to IDPH as 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.250 requires.
policies.policy: When an employee is alleged to have abused, neglected or financially exploited a client, [AGENCY NAME] will immediately remove the employee from direct client contact and will investigate. The agency will complete a written report of findings within 14 days after the initial report. It will send the report to IDPH within 24 hours after the investigation is completed and will keep a copy on agency premises for 12 months. The report will include all required elements. The investigation does not replace reports to the elder abuse provider agency, IDoA or the Area Agency on Aging, the DCFS Child Abuse Hotline, or police, and the agency will make those reports under SAF-01 and SAF-07.

definitions.definition: The first time an allegation is made to or learned by the agency, from any source. The 14-day period starts on this date.
Any work in a client's home, any transport of a client, or any other in-person or one-on-one contact with a client.
The report of findings required under 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.250, with the six elements listed in this policy.

procedures: Any employee who receives or learns of an allegation against an employee reports it to the Agency Manager immediately, and the Manager records the date and time as the initial report. If the Agency Manager is the subject of the allegation, the report goes to [ALTERNATE AGENCY MANAGER] or the governing body.
On receipt, the Agency Manager takes steps to protect the client, including calling 911 where needed (see SAF-07) and confirming the client's medical needs (see SVC-08).

The same day, the Agency Manager removes the accused employee from all direct client contact, with no exceptions. The removal is neutral and is not a finding of guilt. The agency arranges replacement care so the client is not left without services (see SVC-06).

The Agency Manager makes or confirms the required report to the elder abuse provider agency designated by IDoA or the Area Agency on Aging, or the DCFS Child Abuse Hotline if the victim is under 18, under SAF-01, and records the time and name of the person who took the report.
The Agency Manager assigns an investigator who has no conflict of interest and who has not supervised the accused employee. The Manager sets the due date: the 14th day after the initial report.
The investigator preserves evidence, including visit notes, EVV records, schedules, texts and emails, and photographs, and does not allow records to be altered.

The investigator interviews the client or representative (in a manner that respects the client's comfort and rights), the accused employee, witnesses and any other involved person, and records each interview with date, time and who was present. The investigator takes written witness statements.

The investigator coordinates with law enforcement and the elder abuse provider agency, and does not interfere with their work. If police ask the agency to delay interviews, the investigator documents the request.
The investigator documents the injury or abuse, including any medical findings, and reviews the employee's personnel file, training, supervisory visit notes and any earlier complaints (see PER-05).

The investigator completes the written report within 14 days after the initial report. It must contain: (1) dates, times and a description of the incident; (2) a description of the injury or abuse; (3) actions taken by the agency; (4) the individuals and agencies interviewed or notified; (5) action taken to prevent recurrence; and (6) witness statements.

The Agency Manager reviews and signs the report and states whether the allegation was substantiated, not substantiated, or could not be determined. The Manager decides on discipline, which may include termination, retraining, or return to duty, and records the reasons.

Within 24 hours after the investigation is completed, the Agency Manager sends the report to IDPH by [METHOD AS DIRECTED BY IDPH Home Services Program, 217-782-7412] and records the date and method of sending.

If the employee is a Health Care Worker Registry-listed individual and the findings meet the reporting criteria of the Health Care Worker Background Check Act and Code, the Agency Manager takes the steps required by those laws (see PER-02).

The agency keeps a copy of the report and all records on premises for 12 months, in a secure file separate from the personnel file and the client record, with a cross-reference to each (see REC-01 and REC-03).

The Agency Manager tells the client or representative of the outcome and of the steps taken to protect the client, within the limits of confidentiality (see CR-03). The Manager also reviews any needed changes in the client's service plan.
The Agency Manager reviews each investigation in the QI Program and lists actions to prevent recurrence, such as added training or supervision (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Receives allegations, removes the employee from client contact, assigns the investigator, signs the report, sends it to IDPH within 24 hours of completion, and decides on discipline.
Gathers evidence and statements and completes the written report within 14 days of the initial report.
Takes the Agency Manager's role if the Manager is implicated or unavailable.
Report allegations at once, cooperate with the investigation, and keep the matter confidential.

documentation: Record of the initial report (date, time, source)
Record of removal from client contact
Records of reports to the elder abuse provider agency, DCFS or police
Interview notes and written witness statements
Written investigation report with the six required elements
Proof of transmission to IDPH within 24 hours of completion
Copy of the report kept on premises for 12 months

policies.title: Home Services Worker Qualifications and Health Care Worker Registry
policies.applies_to: HR staff, the Agency Manager, supervisors and all home services workers and applicants of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure that every person who works as a home services worker for [AGENCY NAME] meets the Illinois qualification and employment requirements, is cleared through the Health Care Worker Background Check process and has complete documentation on file before being assigned to clients.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will assign a worker to a client only after the file contains the documentation required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.71(a). For a worker who is not otherwise licensed, certified or registered, the file must show: no disqualifying Health Care Worker Background Check, or a waiver; a copy of the Social Security card; and a visa or proof of citizenship that meets federal employment requirements. For any position needing a State professional license, the agency will verify with IDFPR that the license is active before employment and will keep a copy. The agency will comply with the Health Care Worker Background Check Act and Code and will verify each worker's Health Care Worker Registry status each year.

definitions.definition: An employee who provides home services, meaning help with activities of daily living, housekeeping, personal laundry and companionship in the client's residence. These tasks do not require a Nurse Practice Act license.
The IDPH registry of health care workers, which includes results of background checks initiated through IDPH.

A worker who holds a State professional license or other certification or registration, such as a certified nursing assistant on the Registry. Verification rules for these workers differ as described below.
The federal Employment Eligibility Verification form used to confirm identity and authorization to work.

procedures: The agency posts job openings with the minimum qualifications from the job description (see PER-08). Hiring decisions are made by the Agency Manager or a designee with hiring authority.

HR confirms the applicant can perform the essential duties of a home services worker as defined in the job description, and gives the applicant a clear description of the limits of the job (see SVC-01).

Before the applicant has any client contact, HR starts the Health Care Worker Background Check under PER-02 and confirms the applicant's Registry status. The applicant may not be assigned to clients until the check is complete and there is no disqualifying result, or a waiver has been granted.
HR obtains a copy of the applicant's Social Security card and keeps it in the personnel file.

HR completes Form I-9 (8 CFR 274a.2) within the federal time limits. HR examines the original documents and keeps a copy of the visa, proof of citizenship or other documents that show the right to work. I-9 forms are filed in the personnel file or a separate I-9 file, as the agency chooses.

For an applicant who holds a license, certification or registration, such as a certified nursing assistant, HR verifies it as follows. For any position that requires a State professional license, HR verifies with IDFPR that the license is active before employment, prints or saves the verification, and puts a copy in the personnel file. For a CNA on the Registry, HR verifies Registry status and any findings.

A CNA listed on the Health Care Worker Registry may use prior training in place of the agency's initial training. The CNA still receives a competency evaluation before the first assignment (see PER-03 and SVC-11).

The agency does not apply the home health aide training standard of 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.70, because [AGENCY NAME] does not offer home health aide services. Workers are trained and evaluated under the home services worker standard in 245.71 (see PER-03).

HR keeps in the personnel file the worker's name and address, Social Security number, date of birth, next of kin, evidence of qualifications, dates of employment, and, at separation, the reason for separation (see PER-05).

HR checks that the file is complete using the Pre-Assignment Checklist: background check cleared, Registry verified, Social Security card, work authorization, license verification if applicable, health evaluation (see PER-04), orientation, competency evaluation and signed job description. The Agency Manager or HR Coordinator signs the checklist, and only then is the worker added to the schedule.

Each year, HR verifies each worker's Health Care Worker Registry status and any license or certification, and records the date, the person who checked it and the result in the file. This addresses IDPH survey guidance on annual Registry verification.

If a verification shows a new disqualifying finding, an expired or revoked license, or a lost work authorization, HR notifies the Agency Manager the same day. The Manager removes the worker from client contact until the issue is resolved, and arranges replacement care (see SVC-06).
The agency applies these requirements equally to contracted and subcontracted workers (see PER-10 and GOV-07).
HR audits a sample of personnel files each quarter against the Pre-Assignment Checklist and reports results to the QI Program (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Holds hiring authority, confirms that no worker is assigned before the file is complete, and acts on verification problems.
Collects and verifies documents, performs license and Registry verification, completes I-9, and maintains the checklist and files.
Does not schedule workers who lack a cleared checklist.
Provides accurate documents, and reports changes in license, certification or work authorization.

documentation: Health Care Worker Background Check result with no disqualifying finding, or waiver
Health Care Worker Registry verification, including annual re-verification
Copy of Social Security card
Form I-9 and proof of citizenship or work authorization
IDFPR license verification and copy, where applicable
Evidence of qualifications and CNA Registry verification, where applicable
Pre-Assignment Checklist
Quarterly file audit results

policies.title: Background Checks and Health Care Worker Registry
policies.applies_to: HR staff, the Agency Manager, and all applicants, employees and contracted workers of [AGENCY NAME] who are covered by the Health Care Worker Background Check Act
policies.purpose: To describe how [AGENCY NAME] complies with the Health Care Worker Background Check Act (225 ILCS 46) and the Health Care Worker Background Check Code (77 Ill. Adm. Code 955), and how the agency uses and verifies the Health Care Worker Registry, as required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.72.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will complete a fingerprint-based Health Care Worker Background Check for every covered applicant and employee, and will check the Health Care Worker Registry, before the person's first client assignment. The agency will submit fingerprints promptly, no later than 10 working days. It will not assign a worker with a disqualifying result unless a waiver has been granted. It will keep results in the personnel file. It will maintain access to the IDPH Registry, which is required with the license application, and will verify each worker's Registry status each year.

definitions.definition: The fingerprint-based criminal history check required by 225 ILCS 46 and 77 Ill. Adm. Code 955 for covered health care workers.
The IDPH registry that records results of background checks initiated through IDPH and other information about health care workers.
A conviction or finding listed in the Act and Code that bars a person from working in covered positions unless a waiver is granted.
A decision under the Act and Code that allows a person with a disqualifying offense to be employed. The process and conditions are in 77 Ill. Adm. Code 955.

procedures: Before the license application is submitted, the Agency Manager sets up the agency's access to the IDPH Health Care Worker Registry and confirms the access in writing. Proof of access to the Registry is included in the application package, along with this written background check process.

The Agency Manager designates the person or persons authorized to use the Registry and run checks. Each person signs a confidentiality statement, and results are limited to those who need them for hiring decisions (see CR-03 and PER-05).
HR tells each applicant, in the job offer and application, that employment depends on a background check and that the check is required by Illinois law.
