HR has the applicant complete the consent and application forms required for the check. HR confirms the applicant's identity against a government-issued photo ID.

HR arranges fingerprinting through a live-scan or other approved vendor listed in 77 Ill. Adm. Code 955 and confirms the fingerprints are sent to the Illinois State Police. The agency's standard is to submit within 10 working days. HR records the date of submission and any tracking number.
HR checks the Health Care Worker Registry for the applicant and records the date of the check and its result before the first assignment.
The applicant may not have client contact, or be placed on the schedule, until the check is complete and HR has recorded a result with no disqualifying finding, or a waiver has been granted.

Where results show a possible disqualifying offense, HR gives the Agency Manager the result the same day. The Manager reviews it against 77 Ill. Adm. Code 955, which also sets how long results remain valid and the waiver process. The Manager tells the applicant and, where the Code permits, helps the applicant apply for a waiver. The agency does not employ the person in a covered position unless a waiver is granted.

The agency treats the applicant's criminal history information as confidential. It does not disclose results to other people, and it does not make adverse decisions beyond those the Act and Code require or allow.

HR keeps the background check result and Registry verification in the personnel file (see PER-05) and records the check date, who did the check and the outcome on the Pre-Assignment Checklist (see PER-01).

For employees on staff, HR re-verifies Registry status at least once each year, in the same month for all staff, and records the date, who checked, and the result. IDPH surveyors treat annual Registry verification as a common deficiency area.

The Agency Manager requires that employees notify the agency right away if they are charged with or convicted of a criminal offense. HR reviews the matter with the Agency Manager and removes the employee from client contact if the facts warrant it.

For contracted or subcontracted workers, the agency requires the same background check and Registry verification before assignment, and verifies it by obtaining a copy of the result or checking the Registry directly (see PER-10 and GOV-07).

HR audits a sample of files each quarter for complete background checks and timely annual verification, and reports gaps to the Agency Manager and the QI Program (see GOV-04). The Manager corrects gaps immediately.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains Registry access, decides on questionable results, handles waivers, and ensures no uncleared worker is assigned.
Starts fingerprinting, checks the Registry, records results, performs annual verification and audits files.
Does not schedule a worker without a cleared background check.
Cooperate with the process and report new charges or convictions.

documentation: Written background check process (part of the license application package)
Proof of access to the IDPH Health Care Worker Registry
Consent forms and fingerprint submission record with dates
Background check results and Registry verification in the personnel file
Waiver documents, where applicable
Annual Registry re-verification record
Quarterly audit results

policies.title: Orientation, Competency Evaluation and Annual Training
policies.applies_to: All home services workers, home services supervisors and trainers, and the Agency Manager
policies.purpose: To make sure every home services worker is trained and shown to be competent before serving clients, and stays current through annual training, as 77 Ill. Adm. Code Part 245 requires for a Home Services Agency licensed by IDPH.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides or arranges at least 10 hours of initial training for every home services worker. At least 5 hours are completed before the worker's first assignment, and the remaining 5 hours within 30 days of the start of employment. No worker receives a client assignment until the worker passes a competency evaluation on the first 5 hours of topics. A second competency evaluation follows the remaining 5 hours. Each worker then completes at least 10 hours of training in every later year of employment. All training is documented to survey standard. The 8-hour figure that applies to placement agencies is not the standard for this agency. [AGENCY NAME] is a direct-service agency and follows the 10-hour standard.

definitions.definition: The first 10 hours of training given to a new home services worker: 5 hours before the first assignment and 5 hours within 30 days of the start of employment.
A test of the worker's knowledge and demonstrated skill on the topics just taught. The worker must pass it before moving to client assignments or the next training phase.
At least 10 hours of training per year of employment on the topics required for annual training.
The 12-month period used to count annual training. [AGENCY NAME] uses the worker's employment anniversary date.
A person who meets the qualification standard in PER-09 and gives initial training and ongoing supervision.

procedures: The Agency Manager or designee schedules each new hire's first 5 hours of training on or before the first day of employment. The worker is not placed on the client schedule until the first competency evaluation is passed.

The first 5 hours cover orientation to the agency, the Home Services Agency Licensing Act and rules as they affect the worker, job responsibilities and limits (SVC-01), confidentiality (CR-03), client rights (CR-01), abuse, neglect and exploitation reporting (SAF-01), infection control and hygiene (SAF-03), safety and emergencies including first aid and the client's emergency preparedness plan (SAF-04), and observing, reporting and documenting (SVC-08).

The remaining initial content covers communication with people who are hard of hearing or have dementia, personal care tasks including medication reminding (SVC-05), adaptive equipment, keeping a clean and safe environment, understanding dementia, problem-solving for challenging dementia behaviors (SVC-12), the ADL tasks listed in the Part 245 task list, and any other task [AGENCY NAME] assigns to the worker.
A qualified supervisor or trainer gives or approves all training. The trainer's name and qualifications are recorded for every session (PER-09).

After the first 5 hours, the trainer gives a written or skills-demonstration competency evaluation on those topics. A worker who does not pass is retrained on the missed topics and re-evaluated. The worker receives no assignment until a passing result is on file.
The worker completes the remaining 5 hours within 30 days of the start of employment. The trainer then gives a second competency evaluation on those topics, and the result is filed.

Task-specific competency is checked under SVC-11 before a worker performs a task such as bathing, positioning, feeding or nail care. Workers who serve clients on oxygen receive training on oxygen delivery before serving them.

For a worker who presents proof of training from another licensed home services agency within the prior 365 days, or who is a CNA on the Health Care Worker Registry, the Agency Manager reviews the proof against the required subjects. Accepted training is credited in the worker's file. The worker still passes a competency evaluation before the first assignment, and any required subject not covered is taught before the first assignment.

A worker who will serve clients with dementia must complete the dementia subjects in the required training before assignment to such a client (SVC-12). The Agency Manager confirms the dementia training hours required by IDPH before finalizing the curriculum.
The Agency Manager assigns annual training on the worker's employment anniversary basis. Each worker completes at least 10 hours per year. The initial 10 hours satisfy the first year of employment.

Annual training must include: client dignity, independence, self-determination, privacy, choice and rights; disaster procedures; hygiene and infection control; abuse and neglect prevention and reporting; and the ADL tasks in the Part 245 task list, including oxygen delivery for workers who serve clients on oxygen.
Self-study is allowed only if the worker's learning is demonstrated, by a quiz or skills check scored by the trainer, and the material and result are filed.
Each year the Agency Manager verifies the worker's status on the Health Care Worker Registry and confirms the annual education is complete. The check is documented (PER-02).

For every session the trainer records the date, minutes spent on each topic, the instructor's name and qualifications, a description of the content, and the worker's signature or an electronic completion certificate with date and time stamp.

The Agency Manager reviews a training tracking log monthly. Workers whose annual training is due within 60 days are scheduled. A worker who has not completed the annual hours by the anniversary date is not scheduled until the requirement is met, unless the Agency Manager documents a plan to finish within a short, defined period.
Training records are filed in the worker's personnel file (PER-05) and are available to IDPH surveyors on request (GOV-08).
Training content is reviewed annually with the Quality Improvement Program (GOV-04), including incident trends and survey findings, and updated as needed.

responsibilities.duty: Ensure no worker is assigned before passing the required competency evaluation; maintain the training tracking log; verify annual Registry status and education; keep all training records.
Deliver or approve training; administer and score competency evaluations; record date, minutes, content and qualifications; remain available to workers for continuing education.
Complete all assigned training on time, pass competency evaluations, and sign or electronically certify each session.
Approve the training program and provide resources to carry it out.

documentation: Training record for each session: date, minutes per topic, instructor and qualifications, content description, worker signature or time-stamped electronic certificate
First and second competency evaluation results with the evaluator's name and date
Proof of prior training within 365 days, if accepted, with the manager's review note
Annual Registry verification record
Training tracking log
Self-study materials and demonstration of learning

policies.title: Employee Health Evaluation and Communicable Disease Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees who have client contact, and their supervisors
policies.purpose: To protect clients and staff from communicable disease by requiring an initial health evaluation of each new employee with client contact and by setting clear rules for reporting symptoms and exposure, removal from client contact, and return to work.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires an initial health evaluation of every new employee who will have client contact, as specified by the governing body. Employees must report symptoms of, and exposure to, communicable disease. The agency removes employees from client contact under the conditions below and returns them to client contact only when the return conditions are met. Health information is kept confidential and separate from the personnel file.

definitions.definition: A health assessment completed before an employee's first client contact, with content set by the governing body and performed by a licensed health care professional.
An illness that can spread from person to person, such as influenza, COVID-19, gastrointestinal illness, active tuberculosis, scabies, lice or a skin infection that cannot be covered.
Contact with a person or material that carries a risk of transmitting a communicable disease to the employee.
Taking an employee off the client schedule until the return conditions are met.

procedures: Before the first client contact, each new employee completes an initial health evaluation by a licensed health care professional. The evaluation covers the content set by the governing body in [GOVERNING BODY HEALTH EVALUATION STANDARD]. A health evaluation is a condition of assignment to clients.

The governing body defines what the evaluation includes, including whether and how often tuberculosis screening is required. The Agency Manager confirms with IDPH before adopting any TB testing requirement, and the governing body records the decision in its minutes.

The employee gives the Agency Manager written confirmation from the examiner that the evaluation was completed and whether the employee may work with clients. Detailed medical findings are not placed in the personnel file.
The Agency Manager files the confirmation and any results in a confidential employee health file kept separate from the personnel file and locked or access-restricted.
Orientation (PER-03) teaches employees the symptoms that must be reported: fever, cough, sore throat, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, draining or open skin lesions, and any diagnosed communicable disease.

An employee who has symptoms of a communicable disease, or who has been exposed to one, must call the supervisor before the shift, at [PHONE]. The employee must not go to a client's home until cleared by the supervisor.

The supervisor asks about symptoms and exposure, records the answers, and decides on removal using this policy. When in doubt, the supervisor removes the employee from client contact and consults a health care professional or the local health department.

Removal conditions: fever; vomiting or diarrhea; a diagnosed communicable disease in the infectious period; an uncovered draining wound or skin infection; or exposure that the health department or physician says requires exclusion.
The supervisor arranges replacement coverage so the client's visit is not missed (SVC-06), and notifies the client's other workers if they may have been exposed.

Return conditions: the employee is symptom-free for the period set by the health professional or health department, or presents a clearance note from a health care professional, and the supervisor approves return in writing.
For reportable communicable diseases, the Agency Manager notifies the local health department as required by law and follows its directions (REC-02).
If an employee's illness may have exposed clients, the Agency Manager identifies the affected clients, notifies them and their representatives, and records the actions in an incident report (SAF-02).
Employees are not penalized for reporting symptoms or exposure in good faith. Leave policies in PER-06 apply.
The Agency Manager reviews exposure reports at least annually with the Quality Improvement Program (GOV-04) and updates infection control practices (SAF-03).

responsibilities.duty: Specify the content of the initial health evaluation and any TB screening requirement, after confirming with IDPH.
Verify evaluations are complete before first client contact; maintain the confidential health file; make removal and return decisions with the supervisor.
Receive symptom and exposure reports, apply removal conditions and arrange coverage.
Complete the evaluation; report symptoms and exposure before the shift; stay away from clients while removed; provide clearance for return.

documentation: Initial health evaluation confirmation for each employee with client contact
Confidential employee health file, separate from the personnel file
Symptom and exposure report log
Removal and return-to-work records with supervisor approval
Notices to the local health department and affected clients, where applicable
Governing body minutes setting the evaluation content

policies.title: Personnel Records
policies.applies_to: Agency Manager, administrative staff, and all employees and contracted workers whose records are kept
policies.purpose: To keep complete, accurate and confidential personnel records that show each worker's qualifications, background check, training and evaluations and are ready for an IDPH survey.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a personnel record for every employee. Each record contains the items required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code Part 245, and the records are kept confidential. Records are stored on agency premises or in a secure electronic system that the agency can produce for IDPH on request.

definitions.definition: The file for each employee holding identifying information, qualification evidence, training, evaluations and separation information.
A separate confidential file of health evaluations and exposure records (PER-04).
A license, registration or certification where required, or documentation that the worker meets the home services worker requirements.

procedures: The Agency Manager opens a personnel record for each employee before the first day of work and verifies that it is complete before the first client assignment.

Each record contains: name and address; Social Security number; date of birth; next of kin; evidence of qualifications; employment dates; and, when employment ends, the separation date and the reason.

For each worker who is not otherwise licensed, certified or registered, the file also contains documentation of a Health Care Worker Background Check with no disqualifying finding, or a waiver; a copy of the Social Security card; and a visa or proof of citizenship that meets federal employment requirements (PER-01, PER-02).

For anyone in a position that requires a State professional license, the Agency Manager verifies with IDFPR that the license is active before employment and keeps a copy of the verification in the file.
The employer completes Form I-9 within the federal deadlines for each new hire. I-9 documents are kept in the file or in a separate I-9 binder, and retained as federal rules require.

The record contains the job description signed by the employee (PER-08), the initial health evaluation confirmation or a note that it is in the employee health file (PER-04), and the signed acknowledgement of agency policies.

Training and competency records are kept in the file: date, minutes per topic, instructor and qualifications, content, and worker signature or time-stamped electronic completion, plus both initial competency evaluations (PER-03).
The annual performance evaluation and each year's Registry verification are filed (PER-08, PER-03).
Contracted staff files hold the same evidence of required license, registration or certification, and the supervision records (PER-10, GOV-07).

Personnel records are kept in a locked cabinet or access-controlled electronic system. Only the Agency Manager, designee, and persons authorized by law may view them. Employee health information is kept in the separate confidential health file.
Access to records by an employee, IDPH surveyor or other outside party is logged. Copies given to outside parties require the Agency Manager's approval, except where law requires production.
Records are retained for at least five years after separation, unless a longer period is required by law or a pending claim. This period is adopted by the governing body and confirmed with counsel.
The Agency Manager audits a sample of personnel records each quarter against a checklist and corrects any gaps within 14 days. Results go to the Quality Improvement Program (GOV-04).
At separation, the Agency Manager records the separation date and reason and closes the file, which is then archived under the retention schedule.

responsibilities.duty: Maintain complete, current and confidential personnel records; verify licenses with IDFPR; run quarterly file audits.
File documents as directed and keep storage secure.
Give accurate information and notify the agency of changes in address and next of kin.
Approve the retention period and review audit results.

documentation: Personnel record checklist for each employee
IDFPR license verification copies
Background check results or waiver, Social Security card copy and work authorization proof
Form I-9
Training and competency records
Annual performance evaluations
Record access log
Quarterly file audit results

policies.title: Wage, Hour and Overtime Compliance
policies.applies_to: Agency Manager, payroll staff, supervisors and all hourly home services workers
policies.purpose: To make sure workers are paid correctly for all hours worked, as required by federal and Illinois wage law, and that the agency's written personnel policies cover wages, benefits, hours of work and leave.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains written policies on wage scales, benefits, hours of work and leave. The agency pays every worker at least the highest applicable federal, Illinois and local minimum wage. As a third-party employer, the agency does not claim the companionship or live-in exemptions from overtime, and pays overtime for hours worked over 40 in a workweek. Travel time between client visits is paid as hours worked.

definitions.definition: All time the employee is required to work or is on duty, including time with clients, paid training, and travel between clients during the workday.
A fixed, recurring period of 168 hours (seven consecutive 24-hour periods) set by the agency as [WORKWEEK START DAY AND TIME].
Hours over 40 in a workweek, paid at one and one-half times the employee's regular rate of pay.
An employer other than the client or the client's family, such as a licensed home services agency.

procedures: The governing body adopts a written wage scale for each position and a written benefits and leave summary. The Agency Manager gives each employee a copy at hire (245.30 personnel policies).
At hire the Agency Manager tells each worker the hourly rate, the pay period, the pay date, and the workweek used for overtime.

Hourly rates are never set below the highest applicable minimum wage. The Agency Manager checks the federal, Illinois, Cook County and City of Chicago rates each January and July, and adjusts pay as soon as a rate changes. Because local rates differ and adjust each July 1, the Agency Manager confirms the current rate with the Illinois Department of Labor and, where applicable, the City of Chicago.
Workers record time through the EVV and timekeeping system (SVC-07). Workers must not work off the clock, and supervisors may not ask them to.
Paid time includes visit time, paid training and orientation, required meetings, and travel time between clients on the same day. Payroll counts these hours.

Payroll totals the hours worked for each workweek. For hours over 40, the agency pays one and one-half times the regular rate. The regular rate includes any shift differentials or non-discretionary bonuses.

The agency does not treat workers as exempt under the companionship or live-in provisions of the FLSA, as third-party employers cannot claim them (29 CFR 552). Live-in or sleep-time arrangements are approved only by the Agency Manager after review with counsel.

The Agency Manager reviews each schedule before it is released to avoid unplanned overtime. When overtime is unavoidable, it is paid. Overtime is not a basis for discipline when approved by a supervisor.

The agency complies with the Illinois Paid Leave for All Workers Act and any applicable local paid leave ordinance. The Agency Manager confirms current requirements with counsel and writes the leave accrual, use and carryover rules into the leave policy.

Workers who find an error in their pay tell payroll or the Agency Manager in writing. The agency investigates and corrects any underpayment on the next pay date, or sooner if possible. No retaliation occurs for raising a pay concern.
Payroll prepares each pay statement with the hours, rate, overtime, deductions and the pay period. Deductions are made only as required or authorized in writing.
For Medicaid-funded services, pay rates are set by the agency and are not tied to the program reimbursement rate. The agency pays wages as this policy requires, whatever the payer (SVC-10).

The Agency Manager audits payroll quarterly against EVV time records, travel time and overtime, and reports results to the Quality Improvement Program (GOV-04). Findings under this policy are corrected and any back wages paid promptly.
Payroll records are kept for at least the period required by federal and Illinois law, and for at least five years as agency policy.

Monitor minimum wage changes; approve overtime; confirm compliance with counsel; run quarterly payroll audits.
Calculate hours, overtime and travel time; issue accurate pay statements.
Schedule to limit overtime; never require off-the-clock work.
Record all time accurately and report pay errors promptly.

policies.title: Staff Conduct and Professional Boundaries
policies.applies_to: All employees, contracted workers and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To set clear standards of conduct and professional boundaries so that clients are treated with respect, are protected from abuse, neglect and exploitation, and receive only services within the agency's scope.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires every worker to act professionally, respect client rights, and stay within the limits of the worker's job. Workers are trained on job responsibilities and limits. Conduct that is abuse, neglect or financial exploitation of a client is reportable, and the employee is removed from client contact immediately while the matter is investigated. The agency complies with the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and does not tolerate discrimination or harassment.

definitions.definition: The limit that separates a worker's professional role from personal involvement with a client or the client's family.
Money, goods or favors given to a worker by a client or family member, or by a worker to a client.
Misuse of a client's money or property, including borrowing, taking, or using the client's belongings or accounts.
The tasks listed in the client's service plan and permitted for home services workers (SVC-01).

procedures: At hire, each worker receives and signs this conduct policy. The agency covers job responsibilities and limits in orientation (PER-03).

Gifts and tips: workers do not accept money, tips, gifts of value, loans, or inheritance or beneficiary designations from clients or families. A worker offered a gift politely declines and tells the supervisor the same day. The supervisor records it. Small, perishable items such as a shared snack may be accepted only as approved by the supervisor (CR-04).

Money and property: workers never borrow from, lend to, sell to or buy from clients; never use a client's cards, accounts or PINs for personal purposes; and never take or use client property. Shopping or errands with client money are done only as stated in the service plan, with receipts and change returned and logged (CR-04).

Personal relationships: workers do not enter romantic or sexual relationships with clients, do not involve clients in the worker's personal problems, and do not ask clients for favors. A worker who feels a boundary has been crossed tells the supervisor.
Social media and recording: workers do not post about clients, take photos or videos of clients or their homes, or share any client information online (CR-03).
Personal use: workers do not use a client's phone, computer, car, food or other property for personal use, and do not bring visitors, children or pets into a client's home.

Scope of work: workers do only the tasks in the service plan and permitted by SVC-01. They do not give medical care, set up medications, or perform tasks beyond their competency evaluation (SVC-11). A client request outside scope is declined and reported to the supervisor.

Substance use and conduct: workers do not work under the influence of alcohol, cannabis or non-prescribed drugs, and do not smoke in the client's home unless the client's rules allow and the service plan permits.

Respect and non-discrimination: workers treat all clients and co-workers with dignity regardless of race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age, disability or other protected status. Harassment, including sexual harassment, is prohibited. Complaints are made to the Agency Manager at [PHONE] or to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] (CR-05).

Suspected abuse, neglect or financial exploitation by any person must be reported by the worker to management and to the elder abuse provider agency or IDoA, as set out in SAF-01. Mandated-reporter duties are not delayed for agency review.
If an employee is the alleged perpetrator of abuse, neglect or exploitation, the Agency Manager removes the employee from direct client contact immediately and begins the investigation under SAF-08.
Workers who see another worker violate this policy must report it to the Agency Manager. Retaliation against a reporter is prohibited and is itself grounds for discipline.
Violations lead to discipline, up to and including termination, according to the agency's discipline procedure. Conduct that may be a crime is referred to law enforcement (SAF-07).
The Agency Manager reviews conduct concerns and outcomes during quarterly Quality Improvement Program meetings (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Enforce this policy, handle reports, decide removal from client contact, and refer matters to investigation or law enforcement.
Coach workers on boundaries, receive gift and boundary reports, and document them.
Follow this policy, stay within scope, and report violations and suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation.
Approve this policy and support enforcement.

documentation: Signed conduct policy acknowledgement
Gift and boundary report forms
Receipts and shopping logs for client funds
Discipline and corrective action records
Removal-from-contact records
Conduct reports reviewed under quality improvement

policies.title: Job Descriptions, Performance Evaluations and Hiring Authority
policies.applies_to: Agency Manager, supervisors, and all employees
policies.purpose: To make sure every position has a written job description, every employee has an annual performance evaluation, and hiring is done by the Agency Manager according to those job descriptions.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written job description for every position it uses. The Agency Manager hires qualified personnel according to those job descriptions. Every employee receives a performance evaluation at least once a year. The service agreement tells clients that the agency, and not the client, hires, fires and disciplines workers.

definitions.definition: A written statement of a position's title, duties, limits, reporting line and minimum qualifications.
A documented review of an employee's work against the job description, including competency and conduct.
The authority to select, hire, discipline and terminate employees, held by the Agency Manager under the governing body's direction.

procedures: The Agency Manager writes a job description for every position, including Agency Manager, home services supervisor, trainer, home services worker, scheduler and office staff. Each states title, reporting line, duties, limits, qualifications and physical requirements.

The home services worker job description lists the permitted tasks and clearly states the tasks workers may not do (SVC-01). The supervisor and trainer descriptions state the qualification standard in PER-09.

The governing body approves all job descriptions. They are reviewed at least annually and updated when duties change. They are part of the IDPH application package and are supplied to IDPH on request (GOV-02).

Before an offer, the Agency Manager checks the applicant against the job description's qualifications, including license verification where a State license is required, the Health Care Worker background check, and Registry status (PER-01, PER-02).
The Agency Manager, or a person the Agency Manager designates in writing, makes hiring decisions. Clients and families do not hire, fire, discipline or set pay for agency workers.
At hire, each employee receives and signs the job description. The signed copy goes in the personnel record (PER-05).

Each employee receives a performance evaluation at least annually, on the employment anniversary. The supervisor completes it using the job description, supervisory visit findings (SVC-04), attendance, competency evaluation results, training completion and client feedback.
The supervisor meets with the employee, reviews the evaluation, sets goals and any improvement actions with dates, and both sign. The employee may add comments.
New employees receive an additional review at 90 days.

If performance is below standard, the supervisor documents a written improvement plan with a time frame. Progress is reviewed and recorded. Continued failure leads to discipline, up to and including termination.
Serious concerns, such as suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, are handled under SAF-01 and SAF-08 without waiting for the annual evaluation.
The Agency Manager keeps a tracking log of evaluation due dates and checks it monthly. Overdue evaluations are completed within 30 days.
The Agency Manager names a qualified person in writing to carry out hiring and evaluation duties when the manager is absent (GOV-01).
The Agency Manager reports evaluation completion rates and common findings to the Quality Improvement Program (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Approve job descriptions and the hiring and evaluation process; evaluate the Agency Manager annually.
Write and update job descriptions; hire per job descriptions; make sure evaluations are completed on time.
Complete evaluations, hold review meetings and document improvement plans.
Perform duties per the job description and take part in the evaluation.

documentation: Approved job descriptions for every position
Signed job description in each personnel record
Annual and 90-day performance evaluations
Improvement plans
Evaluation tracking log
Hiring checklist showing qualification checks
Written designation of the person acting for the Agency Manager

policies.title: Home Services Supervisor and Trainer Qualifications
policies.applies_to: All home services supervisors, trainers, the Agency Manager, the Alternate Agency Manager, and anyone who gives initial training or supervises home services workers
policies.purpose: To make sure every person who trains or supervises home services workers at [AGENCY NAME] meets the qualification standards of 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.71, so that workers are trained and supervised by people with real experience in the tasks they teach.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] employs home services supervisors or trainers who give initial training and ongoing supervision to home services workers. No one may supervise or train workers until the agency has verified and documented that the person meets at least one of two qualification options under 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.71(g): (1) at least 2 years of experience within the last 5 years in home health, home services, facility-based healthcare or home nursing, performing tasks that home services workers are permitted to perform, including help with activities of daily living; or (2) a current supervisory or trainer position with a home services agency, plus training within the past year on the permitted tasks. For option (2), the training must show the general standards of care for each required training topic and must be provided or developed by a professional qualified in that field, such as a licensed or certified professional. Supervisors and trainers must be available to workers for continuing education. All training given must be documented as required by 245.71.

definitions.definition: An agency employee who provides ongoing supervision of home services workers, including supervisory visits and review of worker performance.
A person who delivers or oversees initial or annual training for home services workers. A person may be both a supervisor and a trainer.
Work in home health, home services, facility-based healthcare or home nursing, performing the tasks home services workers are permitted to do, including ADL help.

A person licensed, certified or otherwise recognized in the field of the training topic (for example, a registered nurse or a licensed or certified therapist) who provides or develops training content.
The two alternative qualification routes in 245.71(g): recent experience (Option 1) or a current supervisory/trainer position plus training in the past year (Option 2).

procedures: Before offering a supervisor or trainer position, the Agency Manager reviews the written job description (see PER-08) and confirms it lists the qualification requirements in this policy.
At application, each candidate submits a resume and a signed statement of work history with employer names, dates, titles, and duties for the past 5 years.

The Agency Manager (or designee) verifies the history by contacting prior employers or reviewing pay records, offer letters or training certificates, and records the date, person contacted and result on the Supervisor/Trainer Qualification Checklist.

For Option (1), the reviewer counts at least 24 months of qualifying experience falling within the 5 years before the hire date and records the dates and the permitted tasks (including ADL help) that were performed.
For Option (2), the reviewer confirms the candidate currently holds a supervisory or trainer position with a home services agency and obtains the employer's written confirmation.

For Option (2), the candidate must also provide proof of training received within the past year on the permitted tasks. The proof shows the date, hours, topics covered, and the name and credentials of the qualified professional who provided or developed it.

The reviewer compares the Option (2) training content to the general standards of care for each required worker-training topic. Any topic not covered must be completed through agency-arranged training from a qualified professional before the person supervises or trains on that topic.
If a candidate does not meet either option, the Agency Manager does not assign supervisory or trainer duties. The person may be hired in another role only if the job description allows.
The Agency Manager signs and dates the Qualification Checklist and places it, with supporting proof, in the person's personnel file (see PER-05) before the first supervisory or training assignment.

Each January, the Agency Manager reviews the file of every Option (2) supervisor and trainer. The person must show updated training within the past year on the permitted tasks, or the person is removed from training duties until it is completed.

Supervisors and trainers are scheduled and made available to home services workers for continuing education, questions and consultation. Contact information and availability are given to workers in orientation.

When a trainer delivers any worker training, the trainer records the date, minutes per topic, instructor name and qualifications, a description of the content, and the worker's signature or an electronic certificate with date/time stamp (see PER-03).

When subject-matter content (for example, transfer techniques or dementia care) is taught by a person who is not a supervisor, the Agency Manager confirms that person is a qualified professional in that field and keeps proof of credentials with the training record.

If a supervisor's or trainer's required license or credential lapses, or the agency learns that qualification information was inaccurate, the Agency Manager removes the person from that duty immediately and documents the action.
The Alternate Agency Manager audits a sample of supervisor and trainer files at least annually and reports results to the Agency Manager for the quality improvement review (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Verifies and documents qualifications before assignment; signs the checklist; performs the annual review; removes unqualified persons from duties.
Acts for the Agency Manager when absent and audits supervisor/trainer files at least annually.
Provides accurate work history and training proof; maintains current qualifications; remains available to workers for continuing education.
Ensures the agency has enough qualified supervisors and trainers to meet its client and worker load.

Resume, signed work-history statement and employer verification

Annual qualification review record
Training records for all training the person delivers (date, minutes per topic, instructor and qualifications, content, worker signature or electronic certificate)

policies.title: Contracted and Subcontracted Staff Verification
policies.applies_to: Agency Manager, Alternate Agency Manager, hiring and scheduling staff, supervisors, and any contracted or subcontracted worker or third-party provider used by [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure that any person who provides services for [AGENCY NAME] under a contract meets the same legal and agency standards as an employee, holds the license, registration or certification required for the work, and is supervised by the agency.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] may provide services directly or by contract. Before any contracted or subcontracted worker enters a client's home, the agency must hold a written agreement with the third-party provider and must verify that the worker holds any license, registration or certification required by State or federal law. Where a position requires a State professional license, the agency verifies with the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation (IDFPR) that the license is active and keeps a copy in the file. Contracted workers are supervised by the agency. They must meet the same personnel requirements as employees, including health evaluations, employee health policies, criminal background checks and Health Care Worker Registry checks, and the same training and competency requirements. The agency remains responsible for the quality and safety of services delivered by contracted workers.

definitions.definition: An individual who provides services to [AGENCY NAME] clients under a written agreement with the agency or with a third-party provider, rather than as an agency employee.
An outside business or individual that supplies workers or services to [AGENCY NAME] under a written contract.
Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation, the State agency that issues and tracks professional licenses.
The agency's authority to direct, supervise, schedule, evaluate and remove contracted workers from its clients' services.

procedures: Before using any contracted worker or third-party provider, the Agency Manager determines the role, the services to be delivered, and whether a State professional license, registration or certification is required by State or federal law.
The Agency Manager prepares a written contract using the agency's approved template. No contracted worker may be scheduled until the contract is signed by both parties.

The contract must address: the services to be provided; adherence to agency policies and personnel requirements, including health evaluations, employee health policies and criminal background checks; agency control over the services; notes or documentation of services; charges; liability and insurance; the term of the agreement; signatures; and termination.
The Agency Manager collects from the provider a roster of each worker proposed for [AGENCY NAME] clients, with name, role, and copies of required licenses, registrations or certifications.

For each position needing a State professional license, the Agency Manager or designee verifies on the IDFPR license look-up that the license is active, prints or saves the result with the date and the verifier's initials, and places a copy in the worker's file before first assignment.

The agency obtains proof from the provider, or conducts directly, a criminal background check and Health Care Worker Registry check for each worker as required by agency policy (see PER-02), and reviews the results before first assignment.
The agency obtains documentation of the worker's health evaluation and communicable disease screening consistent with the agency's employee health policy (see PER-04) before first assignment.

The agency provides orientation and verifies required training and competency for each contracted worker in the same way as for employees. If the provider's training does not meet agency standards, the agency provides the missing training and evaluates competency before first assignment (see PER-03 and SVC-11).
The Agency Manager gives each contracted worker the client's service plan, the scope-of-work list and the agency's policies relevant to the job, and records the date given.

A home services supervisor supervises each contracted worker as it does employees, including supervisory visits at the frequency required by agency policy (see SVC-04). Supervisors document each visit.
The contracted worker documents services at each visit, using the agency's visit documentation or EVV process, and submits notes to the agency by the deadline set in the contract (see SVC-07).
The Agency Manager obtains a certificate of insurance and any required evidence of liability coverage from the provider at signing and at each renewal, and keeps it on file.

The Agency Manager tracks license, registration and certification expiration dates in a tracking log and re-verifies with IDFPR before each expiration date. A worker whose license is not active is removed from service the same day.
The agency maintains a personnel record for each contracted worker containing qualifications evidence, dates of service, verifications, training and the reason for separation (see PER-05).

The Agency Manager reviews each third-party contract at least annually and at term end, and reports contracted-worker verification results to the quality improvement committee (see GOV-04 and GOV-07).
If a contracted worker is the subject of an abuse, neglect or exploitation allegation, the agency removes the worker from direct client contact immediately and follows SAF-01 and SAF-08.

responsibilities.duty: Approves all contracts; verifies licenses, registrations and certifications; ensures contracted workers meet the same personnel requirements as employees; maintains the tracking log.
Performs verifications and approvals when the Agency Manager is absent.
Supervises contracted workers, conducts supervisory visits and reports concerns.
Assigns only contracted workers cleared in writing by the Agency Manager.
Supplies accurate credentials and documentation, follows agency policies and cooperates with agency control and supervision.

IDFPR license verification printout or screenshot with date and verifier initials
Copies of licenses, registrations and certifications

policies.title: Client Records and Retention
policies.applies_to: All agency staff who create, access, store or handle client records, including the Agency Manager, supervisors, office staff and home services workers
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] creates, maintains, stores and retains a complete and accurate record for every client, in the form required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245, and keeps related reports for the required time.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a client record for every client served. Each record contains: identifying information; contact information for the client's representative; an emergency contact; the agreed plan of services; a copy of the signed home care services agreement; and worker documentation of each service provided at each visit. Records are kept for at least 2 years after the last date of service, in paper or electronic form. As an agency standard, and to meet HIPAA documentation retention rules and payer requirements, [AGENCY NAME] retains client records and HIPAA-required documentation for 6 years after the last date of service, or longer if the IDoA Community Care Program, the DHS-DRS Home Services Program or another payer requires a longer period. Faxed copies must be on non-thermal paper. Abuse and neglect reports and investigation reports are kept on the premises for 12 months. Records are kept confidential and secure under CR-03 and REC-03.

definitions.definition: The set of documents that includes personal information, emergency notification information, agreed service plans, the home services contract, and documentation of services at each visit.
The date of the final visit or service provided to a client, which starts the retention period.
The signed written contract between [AGENCY NAME] and the client describing services, rates and responsibilities.
Paper that does not fade with heat or time, used for fax copies so that the record stays legible for the retention period.
The worker's record, on paper or electronic, of the services performed at each visit.

procedures: At intake, the intake coordinator opens a client record and enters identifying information (name, address, date of birth, phone), the representative's contact information if any, and at least one emergency contact (see SVC-02).
The intake coordinator places the signed home care services agreement and a copy of the scope-of-services list given to the client in the record on the day it is signed (see CR-06 and SVC-02).
The supervisor places the agreed plan of services in the record before services begin and files each updated plan, with date, when it changes (see SVC-03).

Each home services worker documents the services provided at every visit, on the paper visit note or through the electronic system, before leaving the home or by the end of the shift. EVV data and visit notes are kept together in the record (see SVC-07).
Workers submit paper visit notes to the office by the deadline set by the Agency Manager. Office staff check notes for completeness and file them in the client record within 7 days.

Supervisors review visit notes during supervisory visits and record any follow-up. Entries are never altered or erased. Corrections are made by a single line through the error, with the date and initials of the person correcting.
Paper records are stored in locked cabinets in the agency office. Electronic records are protected by individual user IDs, passwords, access limits by role, and regular backups (see CR-03).

Abuse, neglect and exploitation reports and investigation reports are kept on the agency premises for 12 months from the report date, in a secured file separate from the routine client file, with a cross-reference in the client record (see SAF-01 and SAF-08).

Staff who receive or send faxed client documents use non-thermal paper. If a thermal fax is received, staff immediately photocopy it onto non-thermal paper and file the copy. The originating entity keeps the original for 2 years.

Closed records are marked with the last date of service and the destruction-eligible date (6 years later, or the longer payer period). Closed records are kept in the same secure conditions, on paper or electronically.

Before destroying any record, the Agency Manager confirms the retention period has passed, that no complaint, survey, audit, investigation or litigation hold applies, and that payer rules allow destruction.
Records are destroyed by cross-cut shredding or secure deletion. The Agency Manager records the destruction date, the method, and the client record identifiers in a destruction log.
The agency keeps HIPAA-required policies, procedures, notices, authorizations, and other required documentation for 6 years from the date created or last in effect.
If the agency closes or changes ownership, the Agency Manager arranges continued storage and access to client records for the full retention period and notifies IDPH as required by REC-02.
The Agency Manager audits a sample of open and closed client records at least quarterly for the required contents and reports findings to the quality improvement program (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Oversees the records system; approves destruction; ensures this policy is followed and records are available for IDPH survey.
Opens the client record and files required identifying, emergency and agreement documents.
Files service plans and plan updates; reviews visit notes; completes record audits.
Documents services at each visit accurately and on time.
File documents promptly, secure records, keep the destruction log.

documentation: Client record with all required contents
Visit documentation and EVV data
Retention and destruction log
Quarterly record audit results
12-month file of abuse, neglect and investigation reports
HIPAA documentation retention file

policies.title: Required Reports to the State
policies.applies_to: Agency Manager, Alternate Agency Manager, supervisors, and all staff involved in reporting abuse, neglect or exploitation, licensure changes or renewals
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] makes every report, notice and filing required by the State of Illinois on time, to the right agency, and keeps proof of each submission.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] submits all required reports to the State on time. This includes: reports of reasonable suspicion of abuse, neglect or financial exploitation to the elder abuse provider agency designated by IDoA or the Area Agency on Aging (or to the DCFS Child Abuse Hotline for a victim under 18); the written investigation report for abuse allegations against an employee, completed within 14 days of the initial report and sent to IDPH within 24 hours after the investigation is completed; notice to IDPH within 10 days of any change, using the Facility Information Change Form; written IDPH approval before serving clients in a new county; and a license renewal application filed in time, due 60 days before the license expires. The Agency Manager keeps the IDPH license posted or on file and keeps insurance evidence current. Mandated-reporter duties under the Adult Protective Services Act (320 ILCS 20) remain in force and are not delayed by the agency's internal process. A copy of each report is kept as required by REC-01.

definitions.definition: The agency designated by the Illinois Department on Aging, or the Area Agency on Aging, to receive and respond to reports of abuse, neglect and exploitation of eligible adults.
A person covered by the Adult Protective Services Act (320 ILCS 20), including a client aged 60 or older and a client with a disability within the Act's definition.
The IDPH form used to notify the Department of changes to agency information within 10 days.
The initial license, valid 240 days and extendable by 120 days with substantial progress. The full license expires one year from the end of the month the provisional license was first issued.
The first report of an allegation made to the elder abuse provider agency or other authority, which starts the 14-day investigation period.

procedures: Any employee or volunteer who has reasonable suspicion that a client has been abused, neglected or financially exploited reports it immediately to the Agency Manager (or Alternate Agency Manager) and also to the elder abuse provider agency designated by IDoA, the Area Agency on Aging, or the IDoA Senior HelpLine (1-800-252-8966). The employee's report to the State is not delayed or waived if management is unavailable.
If the client is under 18, the Agency Manager or the employee calls the DCFS Child Abuse Hotline immediately.

The Agency Manager calls 911 or local police immediately for staff-inflicted physical injury, sexual abuse by staff, a crime in the home by another person, or a death other than by disease or natural causes (see SAF-07).

The Agency Manager completes the agency's Abuse/Neglect/Exploitation Report Form on the same day, recording who reported, to whom, the date and time, and the reference number given. The report is kept on the premises for 12 months.
If an employee is the alleged perpetrator, the Agency Manager immediately removes the employee from direct client contact and starts the investigation under SAF-08.
The Agency Manager completes the written investigation report within 14 days of the initial report. The report includes the required six elements (see SAF-08). The Agency Manager signs and dates it.

Within 24 hours after the investigation is completed, the Agency Manager sends the written report to IDPH (Home Services Program, DPH.COOS@illinois.gov, or by the method IDPH directs) and records the date, time, method and confirmation. A copy is kept for 12 months.

When any agency information changes (for example, ownership, name, address, telephone, Agency Manager or Alternate Agency Manager, or governing body contacts), the Agency Manager completes the Facility Information Change Form and submits it to IDPH within 10 days of the change. The confirmation is kept in the licensure file.

Before serving any client in a county not on the agency's license or approved service area, the Agency Manager submits a written request to IDPH and receives IDPH's written approval. No client is accepted or served in the new county until the approval is in the file (see GOV-02).

The Agency Manager records the provisional license issue date, the 240-day expiration date, and the full license expiration date on a licensure calendar. The calendar also shows the IDPH on-site survey window (within 30 days of provisional expiration) and the renewal due date.

At least 90 days before the full license expires, the Agency Manager begins the renewal application using the current IDPH home services application. The application is submitted at least 60 days before expiration, with the current fee by check or money order. The Agency Manager confirms the current fee and form version with IDPH (217-782-7412) before submission, as the application fee has been $1,500 on the current form.
If the provisional license needs an extension because substantial progress has been made, the Agency Manager submits the request to IDPH before the 240-day period ends and keeps the written response.

The Agency Manager keeps the current IDPH license posted or on file at the office and keeps current proof of required insurance coverage. Insurance renewal dates are tracked on the licensure calendar (see GOV-02).

The Agency Manager keeps copies of every submission to the State (reports, forms, application, checks or receipts, confirmations) in a Regulatory Reports file and reviews it quarterly for completeness.
The Alternate Agency Manager is trained on all reporting deadlines and submits reports when the Agency Manager is absent, so that no deadline is missed.
Reporting timeliness and any late or missed reports are reviewed at each quality improvement meeting (see GOV-04) and corrective action is documented.

Makes reports and filings when the Agency Manager is absent; trained on all deadlines.
Report suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation immediately to management and to the elder abuse provider agency or IDoA.
Ensures the Agency Manager has the resources to meet licensing, renewal and reporting obligations.

policies.title: Release, Removal and Confidentiality of Client Records
policies.applies_to: All employees, contracted workers, volunteers, supervisors and the Agency Manager who access, remove, copy or release client records
policies.purpose: To protect the confidentiality of client records and to set clear rules for who may use, remove and release them, so that information is shared only when the client authorizes it or the law allows it.
policies.policy: Client records, on paper or electronic, are confidential. [AGENCY NAME] maintains its office so that physical and electronic records are protected. Staff may access only the information they need to do their jobs. Records may not be removed from the office except as this policy allows. Client information may be released only with the client's (or representative's) signed authorization, or where the law allows or requires disclosure, such as abuse reporting under 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.250 and the Adult Protective Services Act. Clients have a right to access their records under HIPAA, and the agency responds within 30 days. Violations of this policy result in discipline up to termination.

definitions.definition: Individually identifiable information about a client's health, care or payment, in any form.
A signed, dated written permission from the client or legal representative to release specific information to a named person or organization for a stated purpose.
Taking any original or copy of client records out of the agency office, including on laptops, phones, flash drives or paper.
Giving or disclosing client information to someone outside the agency.
A person with legal authority to act for a client, such as a guardian or agent under a power of attorney for health care.

procedures: At orientation and each year, every employee and contracted worker signs the Confidentiality Agreement and is trained on this policy and on CR-03. The signed agreement is kept in the personnel file.
Agency office space is locked when no one is present. Paper records are in locked cabinets, and only authorized staff have keys. Visitors are not left alone in areas where records are kept.

Computers and systems that hold client records require individual log-in credentials, automatic screen lock, encryption where available, and role-based access. The Agency Manager removes system access on the day an employee leaves.
Staff do not discuss clients in public places or where they may be overheard. Staff do not post client information, names or photos on social media or personal messaging apps.

Original client records remain in the office. Only the Agency Manager or a supervisor may remove records, and only the minimum copies needed, for a supervisory visit, a service plan update or a required reporting purpose. Removal is logged on the Record Removal Log with name, date, record identifiers, purpose, and date returned.

Workers carry only the service plan and visit documentation needed for the client's home. Papers are kept with the worker and are not left in vehicles or unattended. Documentation is returned to the office on the schedule set by the Agency Manager.
When a request for release comes from anyone outside the agency, the staff member sends it to the Agency Manager, who verifies the requester's identity and authority before any release.

Except where law permits disclosure, the Agency Manager requires a signed authorization before release. The authorization must state who may receive the information, what is released, the purpose, an expiration date, the client's right to revoke it, and the client's signature and date. The agency does not release on an incomplete form.

Permitted disclosures without authorization include reports of suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation to the elder abuse provider agency, IDoA, DCFS or law enforcement under 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.250 and 320 ILCS 20; disclosures required for IDPH survey and complaint investigation; and other disclosures permitted or required by law. The Agency Manager decides and records the legal basis.
Disclosures to payers and program staff (IDoA Care Coordination Units, DHS-DRS) are limited to what is needed for payment, care coordination and program oversight under the applicable program rules.

A client or personal representative may ask to see or get a copy of the client's record. The request is made in writing or noted by staff. The Agency Manager provides access or a copy, in electronic form if requested and available, within 30 days of the request. If the agency needs more time or denies part of the request under HIPAA, the Agency Manager provides the written notice that HIPAA requires.
The Agency Manager verifies the identity of the person asking for access and checks that a representative has authority to act for the client before giving any information.

For each release, the Agency Manager records on the Disclosure Log the date, the recipient, what was released, the purpose, and the authorization or legal basis, and places the authorization in the client record.

Faxed or emailed client information is sent only to a verified number or address, with a confidentiality cover sheet, and in a secure form where electronic. Faxes are on non-thermal paper (see REC-01).

Any suspected or actual unauthorized access, loss or disclosure of client information is reported to the Agency Manager at once. The Agency Manager investigates, documents the facts, takes corrective action, and carries out the notices required under HIPAA (see CR-03 and SAF-02).
The Agency Manager audits the Record Removal Log and Disclosure Log at least quarterly and reviews findings during quality improvement (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Approves releases, keeps logs, responds to access requests within 30 days, investigates breaches and enforces this policy.
May remove only needed records for supervisory visits, logs removal, and returns records promptly.
Protects records carried to a client's home, never discusses clients outside work need, reports any loss or disclosure immediately.
Secure records, verify identity on requests, route requests to the Agency Manager.
May authorize release in writing and may request access to the client's record.

documentation: Signed Confidentiality Agreements
Record Removal Log
Signed authorizations for release
Disclosure Log with legal basis for each disclosure
Record access requests and the agency's response with dates
Incident and breach investigation reports
Quarterly log audit results
